title: Announcers, Referees & Jersey Combination for Raiders Week 6 Matchup
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 6 home matchup against the Buffalo Bills will be the third consecutive week that Las Vegas plays one of the league's top teams. It is shaping up to be yet another challenging outing for a Raiders team still under construction across the board.
After starting the season on a three-game winning streak, the Raiders are now looking to stop a losing streak in a span of games that rival even the toughest schedules in the league. How Klint Kubiak's team performs on Sunday will tell us a lot.
The Raiders have shown us they are better than the bottom-tier teams, which they weren't for the past few seasons. However, Las Vegas' past two games also confirmed they are not elite like the Chiefs and New England Patriots. How they perform against the Bills will clarify things even more.
Las Vegas faces an uphill battle against the Bills this Sunday. Below is additional information regarding the matchup.
Jim Nantz will take care of the play-by-play duties, while JJ Watt will serve as the game analyst. Tracey Wolfson will be the sideline reporter.
Referee Shawn Smith and his crew will call Sunday's matchup against the Bills . Las Vegas will wear its traditional black jerseys and silver helmets, with silver pants, at home on Sunday.
The Raiders look to clean up the penalties that derailed their chances of being competitive last week against the New England Patriots. Entering Week 5, Las Vegas was one of the league's least-penalized teams. The Raiders will need to play clean football against the Bills.
The Raiders, of course, have several other things to worry about besides the referees or the game. Las Vegas has struggled on both sides of the ball over the past two weeks. Sunday's matchup against the Bills, Las Vegas looks to clean up the mistakes.
One of the few positives from Las Vegas' Week 5 loss is that it made it clear where the Raiders need to get better. It also put additional pressure on them not to let the Patriots beat them twice. Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins explained his thoughts on the matter.
“I think the more you can zoom focus, the more you can make it about one technique or one fundamental that just has to be improved, and then kind of allow the bigger picture to fix itself as a result of that one technique. That's the ideal way to approach it,” Cousins said earlier this week.
“But that analysis is such a big part of getting better, is being able to look at it and say, 'Okay, let's boil this down.' It wasn't 17 plays that all had 17 different reasons why we weren't good enough on those plays. Let's try to think what was a common theme, what was a consistent thing that we struggled with or that we can get better in. If we can do that, that's how I think you can get better, is just having that deliberate analysis that helps you then be more productive at practice."
The Raiders have had two consecutive seasons that included 10-game losing streaks. Although that is unlikely to happen this season, with two games against the Bills and the Los Angeles Chargers, they could quickly find themselves almost halfway there.
As the season continues, Las Vegas still has similarly challenging streaks of games. The Bills may very well be the best team they have faced so far, aside from the Kansas City Chiefs. Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko knows the Bills present several different challenges.
“I think it's a very talented group. They're talented. They're well coached. They have a good scheme. They play very hard. They play fast. They're physically gifted. So, those are guys that present a heck of a challenge for us this week. It's something that we're going to attack different ways, but we're excited for the challenge. Those guys are a really talented group,” Janocko said before practice this week.
The Raiders have to find a way to snap out of it before what has happened in the past two weeks continues over the next two weeks.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders' Red Zone Report: Why Drives Stalled, Improvements for Bills
full_text:
After ranking near the top of the league in average points per game, the Las Vegas Raiders' offense has seemingly been figured out. Injuries to an already questionable group of wide receivers and to some of their best offensive weapons have made life difficult for Las Vegas' offense.
On paper, the Raiders are only missing Jack Bech. Brock Bowers missed the first few weeks of the season but is back now. Las Vegas played games without a starting wide receiver, and their starting running back, Ashton Jeanty, is far from healthy.
The Raiders' blowout loss to the New England Patriots witnessed nearly everything that could go wrong, going wrong. However, Las Vegas has consistently failed to do several things the Patriots and the Kansas City Chiefs capitalized on, as will other teams moving forward.
Las Vegas' offense is beginning to show many of the same problems it did in recent seasons. This proves the Raiders are still dealing with the consequences of prior coaching staff and roster decisions.
Entering the season, Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff knew the roster still had several holes to fill. They also knew that many of those holes were unlikely to be addressed until after the season ended. Still, Las Vegas' Week 5 outing left much to be desired.
The Raiders have to do a better job of working with what they have. One challenge is that Las Vegas' first-year coaching staff is largely still figuring out what their team is. Earlier this week, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak shared his thoughts on his team's struggles over the past two weeks.
"I think that you do what you got to do to win the game, man. Your weaknesses come out, and what the numbers say that they are, and we're just trying to go win the game. So, we're trying to improve all of our weaknesses,” Kubiak said earlier this week.
“That's offensive, defense, special teams, and the other side of the ball, they're going to come after what you're good at. They're going harp on, 'Hey, this team, they've taken the ball away,' so they're going protect it better. So, we've got to continue to take the ball away and just continue to improve as a team."
Offensively, Las Vegas' issues are clear and becoming more apparent each week to opposing teams. The Raiders' inability to run the ball made it easy for the Patriots to limit offensive drives. New England shut down the run and pressured Kirk Cousins all day long.
That is the blueprint to beating the Raiders. Make Cousins beat you. Then make sure he does not. Until Las Vegas figures out how to run the ball consistently, many of their offensive drives will resemble what they did against the Patriots.
Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko recently explained that it is up to him and the Raiders' coaching staff to do a better job of putting their players in a better position to succeed. Yet the problem may be that they do not quite have a good enough roster to beat the elite.
Las Vegas' coaching staff will have its work cut out, as Buffalo is just as good, if not better, than any team the Raiders have faced this season.
“I think it comes down to us as coaches putting guys in the best situations possible, understanding the situations, and then executing those plays,” Janocko said earlier this week.
“So, there's things that we evaluate after every game, wins and losses that we can be ready for, and then how do we adjust for unscouted looks and things that you haven't seen. So, and then just being able to let the players play fast and have answers to the test."
Week 6 will be the next chance to see if the Raiders can make the necessary corrections as a coaching staff. For the players, Week 6 will be their next chance to show they are coachable and have the physical capabilities to execute the game plan at a high level.
Time will tell whether the Raiders fare better against the Bills than the Patriots and Chiefs, or if they will lose for the third week in a row.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders' Final Injury Report Paints Interesting Picture
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders continue to work their way through one of the toughest four-game stretches any team in the league has this season. Klint Kubiak's Raiders keep searching for consistency and an identity as they face the league's elite. Sunday, they will host the Buffalo Bills.
The Raiders look to be relatively healthy heading into Week 6. Las Vegas listed 12 players on the injury list throughout the week with various designations. Notably, Tonka Hemingway didn't practice at all this week because he's been dealing with a concussion. He will not play against the Bills.
The Raiders have hit their first bump in the road under Kubiak. After nearly a full week of practice, the first-year head coach believes his team has had a solid week of preparation as they prepare for another team that ranks near the top of the league.
"I've been impressed. That's who they are. They're a very mature group. They want to win, and they know that it takes great practices to win. So, I have been impressed with their response," Kubiak said after Friday's practice.
Brock Bowers, Jalen Nailor, Spencer Burford, Dareke Young, Dont'e Thornton, Segun Olubi, Ashton Jeanty, Patrick Johnson, and Folorunso Fatukasi were all full participants nearly every day this week. They will all be active on Sunday, except for Thornton.
Neither Thornton nor Carter Runyon will play Sunday. Trey Zuhn was a limited participant in practice this week. Kubiak designated the rookie offensive lineman as questionable. Still, the return of their veteran receiver may be a step towards getting the offense back on track .
Nailor's return is huge for a Raiders team with an ailing receiving corps. Even if Nailor does not register big numbers, his presence as a fast, dependable pass-catcher gives the Raiders' offense more of a threat than it has without him. Kubiak explained what Nailor's return means.
“Jalen's [Nailor] a playmaker. He's going to help us. He's going to help us win a lot of games this year, and I think obviously you don't want him to be out for a game, but it gives him a chance to freshen up, and he'll be an impactful player for us."
The Bills are another elite team that does many things the last two weeks have confirmed the Raiders struggle with . Although they are far from fully healthy, Las Vegas appears to be as healthy as it has been since its two-game losing streak started.
The Raiders' Week 5 performance against the New England Patriots solidified the need for improvement in all three phases. Buffalo will do everything it can to capitalize on that on Sunday. Las Vegas' injury report was filled mainly with offensive players.
The unit's overall health is undoubtedly the biggest hurdle the team faces, as it has only added to the unit's struggles, even when healthy. Sunday's home matchup against the Bills is another test early in Kubiak's tenure with the team.
He has been tasked with not only getting the most out of the offense, but also with doing so even when the unit is banged up and still needs further revamping. The Raiders' most recent three coaches struggled with this as well. Kubiak and the Raiders are right on schedule.
Las Vegas is in the first season of a years-long rebuild and is in the middle of a stretch of games against the league's top teams. Las Vegas' areas of improvement are clear. Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko explained the coaching staff's approach.
“Everything we do, we're trying to detail up as we grow in the system, as we grow together as an offense. The individual techniques is something that we emphasize and focus every day, whether it be up front, whether it be with our backs,” Janocko said earlier this week.
“We look at trying to generate more production within the scheme as we look at that, but we take a look at every single aspect, whether it be with the players and their techniques with our scheme, and just trying to grow with every facet of our offense, not just the run game, but we're trying to grow as a full offense together."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Areas of Focus for Raiders in Week 6 Against Bills
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders will return home on Sunday to face the Buffalo Bills at Allegiant Stadium. After dropping their last two games in a row to two of the league's best teams, the Raiders hope to reverse the trend against a Bills team that is just as good as any team Las Vegas has played so far.
There is no shortage of matchups that will factor into Sunday's results. However, the first five games have confirmed that when the Raiders play sound football, they are a tough out. Yet the opposite is true, too. It's clear when Las Vegas is not mentally or physically prepared.
Below are three matchups that will determine Sunday's result.
The Raiders struggled to run the ball for the past three seasons. Nearly halfway through this season, that remains the case. Even after all the changes Las Vegas made to its coaching staff and roster, the Raiders still struggle to run the ball.
As in past seasons, there are several reasons they are struggling to run the ball. The offensive line has struggled to create running lanes, and starting running back Ashton Jeanty is far from healthy. These are just a few reasons Las Vegas has struggled to run the ball.
The Raiders' inability to run the ball over the past few weeks has produced a similar result to past seasons when they struggled to do so. Las Vegas' offense has struggled to move the ball downfield and score points in recent games because it hasn't established a consistent ground game.
It will be nearly impossible for the Raiders to beat the Bills without more success on the ground. With Kirk Cousins' lack of mobility and the Bills' pass rush, failing to run the ball on Sunday will doom Las Vegas. Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko shared his thoughts on the issue.
“We have our calls and we have the different ways that we want to attack different defenses. Every defense gives a unique approach, and we have to have a solution for the different things that they present to us,” Janocko said before practice on Thursday.
“So, whether it's loading the box, light box, different stuff, we really try to give the players the best answer. But it really comes down to us putting the players in their best situations and the guys executing their techniques and playing fast."
The Raiders cannot afford to give up on the ground game too early, even if they do find themselves down big on the scoreboard again. The Bills' offense can get going quickly. The Raiders' offense must help their teammates on defense by sustaining drives.
The Raiders' roster issues that have left them shorthanded at the wide receiver position, and their lack of a ground game, have been caused in part by their offensive line. However, those issues have also hurt the offensive line. The Raiders' offensive struggles go beyond the line.
The Raiders showed what was possible when they protected Kirk Cousins well. Yet with every passing week, it is becoming clearer how quickly pressure can derail this offense. How well the offensive line blocks for Cousins and the Raiders' group of running backs will be a deciding factor.
Cousins must do his part too. The veteran must be more willing to move in a pocket that has been collapsing rapidly lately. It cannot be as easy as rushing more blockers than the Raiders have to derail this offense.
If that is all it takes to derail Las Vegas' offense, they are in trouble for the rest of the season. The only way to fix it is for Cousins to be more mobile, switch up the offensive line, or switch to a quarterback who can move better in the pocket than Cousins.
Depending on how the next two games go, it may be time to start looking at the depth chart for how those potential switches can be made.
Yes, the Raiders started the season with games against some of the league's worst, and their past two games have been against two of the league's best. However, Sunday against the Bills will be just as much about what the Raiders do as the Bills. It may be cliché, but it is true.
The Kansas City Chiefs and the New England Patriots are better than the Raiders. However, the Raiders made a ton of mistakes in both games, which makes it fair to wonder what would have happened had those mistakes been less prevalent. Las Vegas has to take care of their end of things.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders vs. Bills: 3 Key Matchups To Watch
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders and head coach Klint Kubiak are looking ahead to Sunday afternoon at home, where they host the Buffalo Bills, who are coming off a big overtime win against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night.
The opportunity is here for the Raiders to produce an upset. Although they showed flaws against the New England Patriots this past weekend, Las Vegas still has a talented team that can win games. Here are three key matchups that could determine the outcome of Week 6.
This matchup could determine the game on Sunday. The Bills' defensive front isn't the most elite unit, but they have players who can create havoc for some of the Raiders' recent glaring weaknesses. Defensive tackle Deone Walker will be a handful with his rare size and power, especially when he gains leverage at the point of attack; this is a key individual(s) matchup between star center Tyler Linderbaum and guards Spencer Burford and Jackson Powers-Johnson.
The one-on-one matchup I'm intrigued by is Bills edge rusher Greg Rousseau against left tackle Kolton Miller, who has struggled in recent weeks. Miller must do better against power and stout anchoring to stalemate Rousseau, and doing so could give Kirk Cousins more time in the pocket—Las Vegas ranks 15th in Time to Throw average (2.93), according to Next Gen Stats.
I'm combining the entire Raiders defense in this matchup because Josh Allen is that good—he's the best quarterback in football, right up there with Patrick Mahomes. Slowing down his ability as both a passer and run defender is a tall order for any defense, and this poses a defensive coordinator Rob Leonard's biggest challenge.
Allen is second in the NFL in passing EPA (+49.3), second in EPA per dropback (0.30), and third in deep ball percentage (15.9%), according to Next Gen Stats. We all know his abnormal skill set, so will the Raiders need to pray for a chance to slow down No. 17?
I don't think that needs to be the case; the Raiders' defense has the talent to play quarterback containment well and limit rushing production from Allen. The passing defense is the biggest concern, and the biggest question here is how this secondary will rebound from their mauling by the Patriots. Look for the secondary to be aggressive in pass coverage, given Allen's own aggressive tendencies.
Cousins and the Raiders' passing game have a chance to get back on track against a Bills passing defense that is ranked in the bottom 10 in many categories. If there is a game where Kubiak can deploy his wide receivers for productive opportunities, this is it.
Kubiak took responsibility for not giving players like tight end Michael Mayer a better opportunity in the passing game. Brock Bowers has been spectacular, as usual, but Tre Tucker and Cody White have a chance to see touches and make an impact on Sunday.
Look for Kubiak to deploy an aggressive passing attack that could test and strain the Bills' passing defense consistently. A great day in this area, and then the Raiders could be on their way to an upset win, exceeding their win total from last season.

He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. title: How the Waddle Trade Keeps Looking Better and Better for the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sacrificed the present for a better future when they moved Jaylen Waddle in the offseason, but their big trade with the Denver Broncos continues to look good in the moment.
While Waddle had yet another uneventful outing in the Broncos' ugly Thursday night overtime victory against the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday night, the main piece the Dolphins in the trade got some national love Friday morning.
In short, a trade we liked very much from the start has become one we downright love at this point.
To refresh everyone's memory, the Dolphins traded Waddle and a 2026 fourth-round pick (111th overall) to Denver for the 30th overall pick, and picks in the third (94th overall) and fourth rounds (130th overall).
The Dolphins then moved the 30th overall along with the 90th overall selection to the San Francisco 49ers for the 27th overall selection and the 138th overall pick in the fourth round.
With the 27th pick, the Dolphins selected cornerback Chris Johnson, then took wide receiver Chris Bell with the 94th pick, linebacker Trey Moore with the 130th pick and safety Kyle Louis with the 138th pick.
So looking at the complete deal, it comes down to the Dolphins trading Waddle, the 90th pick and the 111th pick for Chris Johnson, Chris Bell, Trey Moore and Kyle Louis.
Oh, and the Dolphins cleared Waddle from their books moving forward, though they did take a $23 million dead cap hit for him in 2026.
It probably will take a couple of years before a final verdict can be rendered on this trade, but the early indications are that it was a big win for Miami.
Regardless of what happened, it helped accomplished the goal of clearing the books beyond this one year of pain, but Waddle's production in Denver through the first six games has eliminated any buyer's remorse.
In Denver's 17-14 victory against Seattle, Waddle had four catches for only 24 yards, the fifth time in six games he failed to top 35 receiving yards.
Since his one big game, a 138-yard performance in Week 2 against Jacksonville, Waddle has recorded 13 catches for 88 yards in the past four games combined.
That four-game stretch is the worst of his career in terms of yardage, not even remotely close to his previous four-game low of 135 yards during the 2024 season.
Waddle was expected to provide the big-play element to a Denver team that reached the AFC Championship Game last year, but instead their offense has faced little but criticism this season even though the team still has a 4-2 record.
Meanwhile in Miami, we also could make the argument that Johnson has performed better, particularly considering he's a rookie.
While the start of his NFL career was bumpy, he has been impressive of late, enough that Sports Illustrated draft analyst Justin Melo mentioned him among his five rookies on the move.
Bell is off to a slow start in his first NFL season, but that's somewhat to be expected considering he's coming back from a serious knee injury and the Dolphins offense as a whole has been dysfunctional.
Moore and Louis are on injured reserve and it's safe to wonder how much they will contribute, if at all, in 2026.
But Moore looked like he was ready in camp to become a major contributor, and Louis will be given a chance at a new position when he returns.
Either way, this trade is looking very good indeed at this time.

title: The Five Dolphins Players Who Must Step Up After the Bye
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins were expected to have a tough time in 2026 given all their roster changes and more importantly their lack of financial resources with so much money committed to players no longer around.
But the expectation also was that there would be gradual improvement and hopefully some measure of success at some point.
At 0-5 heading into their bye weekend without once having a lead, the Dolphins obviously have failed in the success department.
If that's going to change once the Dolphins return to action, starting in Week 7 against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium, they're going to need for some players to start delivering on their promise and raise their level of play.
We'll start with the obvious one because as the quarterback he's the player with the most influence on the final result.
It would be great if Willis got better performances from the people around him and the mistakes and missed assignments would go away, but Willis also has to do his part.
Through the first five games, Willis has shown flashes of brilliance here and there, but there haven't been enough of those while there have been too many missed opportunities. The hope is that Week 5 performance against Cincinnati will end up being the low point for his season and it's all upward from now.
This isn't about Douglas having not performed, he just wasn't around the past three games and it's pretty obvious that maybe he could have made a difference.
In the opener against the Las Vegas Raiders, Douglas showed what kind of factor he could be for Willis and the passing game, and there's just no way to overstate how feeble the passing game has looked since he's been out.
If we are to believe certain analytics like pass rush win rate, Robinson has done just fine so far this season when he's been in the lineup, but the film shows a different reality.
For example, Pro Football Focus gave Robinson a total of four pressures in the Week 5 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals with two hits and two hurries, but the reality is he didn't really affect Joe Burrow because those hits and hurries came after the ball had been released. One example was the touchdown pass to Samaje Perine in the second quarter where Robinson did get to Burrow but from the side and after the ball was released, therefore not affecting the play.
That's what the Dolphins need from Robinson.
It's not about sacks or forced fumbles, but rather affecting the quarterback. One example of that was Willis' first interception where his arm was hit as he threw the ball. That's a real QB pressure and QB hit.
Yes, Robinson has looked better — particularly against Minnesota — this season than he has before, but that should not be the bar for him. The bar for him should be to become an impact player.
Maybe that happens after the bye.
Another one, as with Willis, that seems pretty obvious.
Here, though, there are two reasons it would be very beneficial if Jackson could raise his level of play: The first is it obviously would benefit the offense and Willis; the second is it would help his market value if the Dolphins indeed decide to move him before the NFL trade deadline.
Jackson's work in the run game has been solid, but he really needs to pick it up when it comes to pass protection.
If he doesn't, the Dolphins at some point should and/or will consider removing him from the lineup.
Yes, there are a few other players on offense or defense we could have mentioned here, particularly if we're looking at the big picture, but we're focusing now on winning a game or two.
And the Dolphins aren't good enough right now where they can afford the kind of miscues we've seen from Riley Patterson, whether it's a missed field goal, missed extra point or a kickoff that falls short of the landing zone and gives the opponent the ball at the 40-yard line (he got bailed out against Cincinnati on that last one because of a roughness penalty on the Bengals).

title: Three Reasons for Optimism at the Bye for the Dolphins
full_text:
If you look hard enough, you can find positives from the Miami Dolphins amid their bye week, even if their winless record is enough to write off their season completely.
The Dolphins have fought through adversity, including critical injuries and some of the NFL's best opponents, just to get to their bye week. It might be lost on some how young and inexperienced this roster and coaching staff are, but they've still battled against top-tier talent like Kansas City, Minnesota, and Cincinnati.
Now, they get a week off to rest and recover before a trip to New York to take on the Jets. Miami is still searching for its first win, but a few positives could help them get the job done sooner rather than later.
Anyone who had doubts that Aaron Brewer was not worth the three-year, $52.5 million contract extension is running out of reasons to doubt. All in all, Brewer has been near-flawless to start this season and should be considered one of the best centers in football.
Having clocked 292 snaps, he's been responsible for zero sacks against Malik Willis and has  committed only three penalties. Pro Football Focus has given Brewer an overall grade of 68.2 - the eighth-best out of 34 qualified centers.
What makes Brewer truly stand out is his ability to run block, being a key creator of space for Ollie Gordon II and Miami's ensemble of running backs. His PFF run grade is a 76 flat - the third-best in the NFL. His most impressive performance came against Minnesota - no QB hits, sacks, or penalties, and only one pressure on 39 snaps.
Even more surprising than Brewer, however, has been the resurgence of Jonah Savaiinaea. Many fans were ready to give up on him following a disastrous 2025 season, but switching him back to right guard has helped him grow exponentially.
Clean is the name of the game for Savaiinaea - he's committed no penalties and is responsible for no sacks so far this season on 244 snaps. His performance against San Francisco was as close to perfect as you can get - zero pressures and hurries on 59 snaps.
That said, Savaiinaea suffered an ankle injury in Miami's loss to Cincinnati, and the week off might be just what he needs to recover, but even MORE surprisingly, his replacement was just as effective. Jarrett Kingston came in and held his own, including a noteworthy pancake block on Dexter Lawrence II on his second snap.
There are some fans who might not agree with the decision to draft Kadyn Proctor in the first round, but Proctor has done nothing but justify his selection. It hasn't always been perfect, but you can't deny that only three penalties and one sack through 292 snaps isn't fantastic for a rookie playing left guard for the first time since his freshman season at Alabama.
The major rookie sensation, however, has been linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Through Week Five, he leads the NFL in tackles (57). He's also recorded three tackles for a loss, a pass deflection, and is one of 25 linebackers with an interception. These are first-round numbers being done by someone who was picked 43rd overall, and justify consideration for the Defensive Rookie Of The Year Award.
Chris Johnson might have had a shaky start to the season, but he's ramped up his play since Week Three. When playing in man coverage, he's allowed seven receptions (sixth least in the NFL), 29 receiving yards (third least), and 4.1 yards per catch (second least).
Caleb Douglas was looking like the answer the Dolphins needed at wide receiver following a stellar performance against Las Vegas in Week One, racking up 94 yards on five receptions. Unfortunately, an ankle injury he suffered the following week has sidelined him up to this point, and for Miami's sake, they'll want him back as soon as possible.
Douglas, alongside Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe, has been part of a rookie core that has shown potential for years to come, and the Dolphins still have Kyle Louis and Trey Moore in the stash. All in all, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan did a solid job finding rookie talent in his first season for the Dolphins, which is raising expectations for Miami in a possible make-or-break 2027 Draft.
It would have been easy to write off Miami's running game following De'Von Achane's ACL injury that he suffered against Kansas City. It admittedly looked shaky the rest of the way against the Chiefs, but they got things under control not long after.
The credit goes to the aforementioned offensive line alongside Ollie Gordon II, who has turned into a reliable starter for the Dolphins with 236 rushing yards and three touchdowns, leading the team in both categories. Since becoming Miami's starter, he's averaged 5 rushing yards per attempt, which is the eighth-most in the NFL.
He's been a drive extender, responsible for nine first downs and seven explosive runs, which are runs that net 10 yards or more. He had a brief scare in the Cincinnati game, going to the blue medical tent midway through the game, but returned not long after.
It hasn't all been perfect, however. Jaylen Wright hasn't been an effective backup, with Willis having to do more with his legs to partially compensate. We'll see if the Dolphins continue to stick with Wright as the second option in the backfield or look somewhere else - they missed their opportunity with Jerome Ford, who had a tryout for Miami but ended up signing with Arizona's practice squad.
At the end of the day, the Dolphins average 126.6 rushing yards per game, the 11th-most in the NFL. It could have been much worse considering the loss of Achane, but Gordon has done more than enough to carry the offense on his back at times.

title: Dolphins Thursday Mailbag: Proctor, Willis (Again), Slowik, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of the bye week Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Alain, why do you think everyone (fans, local media) are so desperate to have an opinion and to prove “they are right” about this team and Malik and who to draft. As bad as it is, it’s just five weeks over one season, no??
Hey Salvador, you are absolutely right in that it’s only been five weeks, but this is 2026 and everybody (myself included) needs to have a take on every important topic, whether it be Malik Willis, Jeff Hafley, anything.
Would love to ask Hafley what he seen in his time in Green Bay in regards to Willis that he is not seeing now because this can’t be the guy he seen on a daily basis & decided to bring here with him.
Hey Dave, it’s possible that the answer would be that he doesn’t have anywhere near the supporting cast he had in Green Bay and therefore figures he needs to do much, and at times is trying too hard to make something happen instead of just settling for the simple decision.
Greetings Alain! Doubting Willis’ ability to be a starting QB. Couple of grumpy old man questions, but always a fan. Is it the previously fired OC? Is it the previously fired passing coordinator? At least Chargers are 0-5 too. Thoroughly enjoyed Monday's Dolphins Collective & All Dolphins Podcast. But still looking forward to both the rest of the week plus always all written content on SI.Com.
Hey Dave, I don’t know if I’d pin the issues Malik Willis has had so far this season on either Bobby Slowik and/or Kevin Patullo, but I totally get fans being skeptical of two coaches who landed in Miami after they were fired by their previous employer — and not because of a regime change, where it’s more understandable. There will come a time, maybe sooner rather than later, where we will have to take a long, hard look at the Slowik, though, if the passing game continues to be this substandard.
Will Slowik make some changes and adjust the offense, or will there be more lip service going forward? I feel oftentimes teams or coaches will say that, we will evaluate things, and then nothing really changes.
I think what’s needed more than schematic changes right now is more time between Malik Willis and his receivers so they’re on the same page way more than they have been. I also think the return of Caleb Douglas could provide a big boost for the offense. Maybe the Dolphins will lean even more on the running game in the next couple of games, but I don’t foresee major changes yet.
Hey Alain! Reflecting on the first 5 weeks, this is about what I was expecting. It hasn't been good, but also not a complete disaster like first quarter of the 2019 season. I'm optimistic we will see continued growth from this team as the season progresses. What say you?
Absolutely agree with you, and I wrote as much in a column I posted Wednesday. The start has been rough, but you can’t tear down the roster, wind up with as many young and/or unproven players as the Dolphins have, and expect the team to win a lot of games. That’s simply not realistic.
I know it’s only one game but Kingston didn’t seem like a problem. Is it possible that when Jonah comes back that inserting him into the lineup, and removing Jackson puts your five best offensive linemen on the field? Yes, that would involve moving Proctor to the RT position.
Hey Dana, while I agree with you with Kingston looked the part against the Bengals and that Jackson (obviously) has struggled, I have a very hard time believing the Dolphins are going to do anything at all with Kadyn Proctor in 2026 in terms of a position switch. And I tend to agree with them. Let him go through the full season at guard and then have him work at right tackle from the start of the OTAs. Now, having said, I wouldn’t necessarily be shocked by a switch at right tackle, but that one would have the Dolphins taking a look at what Caedan Wallace can do at that position.
Who do you think potentially gets traded during the trade deadline? Obviously many are speculating Sieler and Jackson, but do you think there could be a sleeper trade candidate that we aren't talking about? Thank you.
Hey Steve, I addressed the trade candidates in the Wednesday mailbag, and the names included were Sieler, Jackson, Josh Uche and Greg Dulcich. I have a hard time picturing anybody else being a trade candidate because I don’t know who else would be appealing to another team understanding they’re not moving any of their key young pieces.
Hey Alain, is it fair to say that if Malik Willis was already on the roster and under contract and not personally hand-picked by Sully and Hafley, that he would have gotten benched at least once during the first five games to at least get a look at what they have in QB2 (McCord)? Not saying that Willis should be benched completely and lose his job, but in a season in which we are going through a complete rebuild I don't see the harm in giving the backup quarterback a little work here and there. It actually seems like the right thing to do considering the talent or lack thereof on the roster. I really don't want to hear much about the lack of receiver talent that he's working with, because an open receiver is an open receiver, I don't care whose name is on the back of the receiver's jersey. Willis is just not seeing them for some reason. Maybe another quarterback will be able to identify the receiver who's open faster. Also it's kind of sad to see his body language when he's sitting on the bench sulking, instead of talking with Slowik, his receivers and O-linemen about what's going on or having his head buried in an iPad the way you see the All-Pro quarterbacks in this league like Allen, Burrow, Mahomes, etc,, doing. Thank you and keep up the excellent work.
Hey Toby, thanks for the kind words. I don’t think there would have been a change at quarterback regardless under your hypothetical, though maybe McCord would have gotten snaps at the end of maybe the San Francisco game. I don’t necessarily believe it’s generally a great idea to bench a quarterback unless you’re ready to make a change, and even had he been an incumbent I have a hard time believing that Kyle McCord would do much better. I get the fascination with McCord because he’s an unknown commodity and maybe he’ll become the great steal all fans want, but the reality is this a second-year sixth-round pick who hasn’t taken a snap in an NFL regular season game yet. I’ve seen those guys play before, and almost invariably it’s not pretty.
Hi Alain, longtime listener and reader of your work. My question has to do with Kadyn Proctor and his position. The current administration seems pretty set on keeping him at left guard and not cross training him at right tackle (which seems like a more valuable position than LG). One thing that hasn’t come up is the possibility that the Dolphins don’t want to give Patrick Paul a huge contract extension in two years and are banking on letting him leave and replacing him with Kadyn Proctor at left tackle. Is there precedent for this at Green Bay while Sullivan was there? Did they always pay their successful drafted linemen to long-term contracts or try to draft their replacements? Have you heard the coaches or administration actually say they are interested in playing Proctor at right tackle? Would love to hear your thoughts.
Hey Daniel, let me start with the last thing first, and the answer is I've never heard Sullivan or Hafley ever discuss Proctor as a right tackle specifically, they just went with the flow of the questions and talked about his development in general. Forget about two years, Paul becomes eligible for an extension after this season and don't think his agent won't be calling Sullivan if he has a strong 2026 season. The Packers generally have rewarded their drafted offensive linemen if they perform.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis…

title: Why Jeremiah Smith Would Be the Perfect Pick ... For a Team Other than the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins appear headed for a very early pick in the 2027 NFL draft and the idea of being able to land Ohio State superstar wide receiver Jeremiah Smith is one that's become very popular among fans as well as mock drafters.
It makes sense considering Smith is pretty universallly recognized as the top prospect in college football at this very early stage of the draft process, and we're talking about a Miami Dolphins team in the early stages of a rebuild that could use help at just about every position.
Going strictly with the BPA (best player available) approach, Smith should be a no-brainer if the Dolphins have the chance to draft him and bring home the Miami Gardens native.
Except it's not that simple.
And we'd suggest the Dolphins would be better off going in another direction.
Through Week 5, the Dolphins hold the third position in the 2027 draft because their combined opponent winning percentage is higher than that of the other two 0-5 teams, the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers.
But according to ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI) projections, the Dolphins have a 49 percent chance of ending up with that No. 1 overall pick, easily outdistancing Tennessee at 20 percent and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at 8 percent.
Because the Dolphins need volume, maybe a best-case scenario if they do end up with the first overall pick would be to trade a few spots in the first round with a team desperate to land Smith or whoever emerges as the top quarterback prospect by next spring, pick up additional assets and still land a high-end prospect to help build their foundation.
If they stay put, whether at No. 1, 2 or 3, it says here the Dolphins would be better served by taking either a quarterback (if they decide that Malik Willis is not going to be the long-term solution and the jury still should be out on that even though things aren't off to a great start) or a player at a different position.
Based on today's NFL, it's pretty well acknowledged that the most valuable positions are quarterback, tackle, pass rusher and cornerback falling somewhere behind that.
Outside of quarterback, there might not be a position in football that's as dependent on the other 10 players on the field as wide receiver because no matter how great, a wide receiver needs a quarterback to get him the ball and an offensive line (usually) that gives the quarterback enough time to do that.
A wide receiver also touches the ball at most, say, 15 times a game, limiting his ability to make a game-changing play — though there is something to be said for the attention a player can draw, which opens up other things for the offense.
This doesn't necessarily prove anything, but the stats remain pretty vivid when it comes to wide receivers and making Super Bowl champs.
The previous 10 winners — Kansas City three times, Philadelphia and New England twice, Tampa Bay, the L.A. Rams and most recently Seattle — featured in their starting lineup a total of 13 players who entered the NFL as a top 5 pick.
Only one of them was a wide receiver. And that wide receiver, Sammy Watkins of the Kansas City Chiefs in 2019, wasn't drafted by that team, but rather by the Buffalo Bills five years earlier.
The list also included four quarterbacks (Tom Brady, Carson Wentz, Matthew Stafford, Sam Darnold), one running back (Saquon Barkley), one offensive tackle (Lane Johnson), two edge defenders (Chris Long, Von Miller), one defensive tackle (Ndamukong Suh), one linebacker (Devin White) and two cornerbacks (Jalen Ramsey and Devon Witherspoon).
Only four of those 13 top 5 picks who won the Super Bowl in the past 10 years won with their original team: Wentz, Johnson, White and Witherspoon. One quarterback, one tackle, one linebacker and one cornerback.
And there's this other statistical tidbit, which might not mean anything but then again might.
In the 15 drafts between and 2024, 12 defensive ends/edge defenders were selected among the first five picks. Ten of those players made the playoffs with their original team, an 83 percent hit rate.
During that same time period, eight cornerbacks went in the top 5 and six of them made the playoffs with their original team, a 75 pecent clip. That was the same percentage at QB with 18 out of 24.
For wide receivers, the percentage was 57 percent, with four of seven wide receivers taken in the top 5 making the playoffs with their drafting team. Those who did were A.J. Green, Amari Cooper, Corey Davis and Ja'Marr Chase. Those who didn't were Justin Blackmon, the aforementioned Sammy Watkins and Marvin Harrison Jr.
And now Harrison has been traded in his third season in the NFL, going from the Arizona Cardinals to the Houston Texans for a second-round pick along with a late-round swap.
This was the same Marvin Harrison Jr. who was considered almost a sure-fire star prospect when he came out of Ohio State in 2024. He wasn't viewed quite as favorably as Smith is these days, but his failure with the Cardinals still should serve as a warning that there are few sure things.
This is where we bring up Calvin Johnson, as perfect a wide receiver prospect as there ever was with his 6-5 stature, 4.2-4.3 speed and great route-running ability. Johnson absolutely was as good as advertised on his way to becoming a first-ballot Hall of Fame selection.
The Detroit Lions selected second overall in 2007 and had no reason ever to regret the pick.
The Lions made the playoffs twice in Johnson's nine seasons.
They never won a playoff game with him.
None of that is Johnson's fault because it takes way more than one great wide receiver to succeed.
But it does show that a brilliant wide receiver isn't enough, even with Matthew Stafford as the quarterback.
The Dolphins found that out the hard way the past several years because it's difficult to envision a more impactful than Tyreek Hill, who was the embodiment of an explosive player who opened things up for the entire offense because of the attention he demanded.
And with Hill — not to mention a great sidekick in Jaylen Waddle — the Dolphins won exactly zero playoff games in four years.
And this is where Smith supporters and/or Hill detractors will point out that Hill shrunk in big moments or simply didn't have the size to operate when the game got more physical, and there is merit to that argument.
By all indications, this won't be an issue with Smith, who's not only got the athleticism but also the size.
What Smith doesn't have is the right position.
If the Dolphins suddenly found themselves only a wide receiver away from contention by next spring, we'd be on board with taking him at No. 1, No. 2, whatever.
But they won't be, so we're not.
Jeremiah Smith is a fabulous prospect and more than likely will become a great NFL player. The Dolphins still should look elsewhere to max out their anticipated top pick in the 2027 NFL draft.

title: Why This Disappointing Dolphins Season Actually Isn't That Disappointing in the Big Picture
full_text:
It's been a rough start for the Miami Dolphins in this 2026 season, the 0-5 record bad enough in itself but made worse by the fact the team hasn't had a lead for even one second in 300 minutes of game action.
It's absolutely been rough to watch, but there are two questions that need to be asked, or rather two points that need to be made.
The first one is pretty simple: Is the Dolphins' bad start really start surprising?
The second is more important: Has it changed the overall outlook for the franchise at all?
The Dolphins' struggles basically boil down to not having enough talent on their roster and also having an awful lot of inexperience with some players who do have enough talent.
And a roster full of young players usually means the kind of mistakes that veteran teams don't make, whether it be untimely penalties or missed assignments.
It's not a big secret that the roster would be deficient this season became GM Jon-Eric Sullivan himself discussed the lack of depth more than once in the buildup to the regular season.
Most of it, of course, was a conscious decision by the organization to reset the salary cap heading into 2027 and that meant getting rid of most of the front-line players who could have helped the Dolphins win some games this year.
The Dolphins' roster moves this year all have been about trying to unearth some hidden gems in the form of young players looking to break through or failed former high draft picks looking to revive their career.
With all of the player acquisitions other than QB Malik Willis, though, the common them has been operating on the cheap.
And, as the old saying goes, you get what you pay for.
What the Dolphins are experiencing right now is a lot of growing pains and paying the price for blowing up the roster, and head coach Jeff Hafley said more than once this season was about more than wins and losses — maybe in large part because he, Sullivan and the entire organization knew full well there likely would be way more losses than wins.
The 2026 season, as we wrote in the offseason, was about the progress and development of the young players who hopefully will form the core of a contender sooner rather than later — a group that included Miami's entire rookie draft class as well as recent high picks like Chop Robinson, Kenneth Grant and Jonah Savaiinaea.
It also was about building a foundation, identity — or culture, if you prefer that term. It's about the new Dolphins way, not to be confused with the Green Bay way because Hafley and Sullivan want to put their own stamp on the Dolphins.
And it also was about evaluating Willis to see whether he could become the long-term answer at quarterback.
Looking at those three objectives, there have been enough good performances from young players through the first five games to take some encouragement, the list including Jacob Rodriguez, Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Michael Taaffe, Trey Moore in training camp, with Robinson showing some improvement.
In terms of building an identity or foundation, that's going to be a work in progress and it obviously will be easier once there's some success in the form of a win or two, though there have been positive signs already based on how the Dolphins have competed.
With Willis, the early returns haven't been very impressive, but there never was a guarantee he was going to be the guy and there's also a lot of time left in this 2026 season for him to provide those signs — because the Dolphins aren't about to pull the plug on his audition anytime soon. Let's also understand that Willis' performance should improve the more time he spends with his teammates on offense, though he does need to stand out on his own merits.
The bottom line is we stand right now about where we were at the start of the regular season, except with five losses, some good performances from some rookies, not nearly as good a start from Willis as hoped, but in the big picture pretty much in the same place.
So, yeah, the 0-5 start does kind of stink a little bit. But this season always was going to be a starting point as the early part of a rebuilding project.
And all things considered, things aren't so terrible because they're not entirely unexpected. And that, like or not, is a better place to be than constantly underachieving.

title: Dolphins Week 6 Power Rankings Roundup: Race for No. 1 Pick Starting to Form
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins remained winless with their loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, a game that wasn't as close as the 31-24 final score might have suggested, and they now stand as one of three teams with an 0-5 record.
If we're not already there, it won't be long before we start focusing on the 2027 NFL draft and more specifically exactly how high the Dolphins' first-round pick will end up being.
Based on the latest round of national media power rankings, they'll have stiff competition for the No. 1 overall pick from the Tennessee Titans.
The Dolphins came in at 31st in the Week 6 power rankings among our 10 national outlets — Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, The Athletic, NFL.com, USA Today, Pro Football Talk, FOX Sports, The Sporting News, CBS Sports — with an average ranking of 31.2 compared to 31.5 for the AFC South team.
For a second consecutive week, the Dolphins did get a ranking as high as 29th, that coming from Nick Shook of NFL.com.
Before we get to our weekly rundown of the Dolphins placement in the rankings with the accompanying commentary, we'll again examine the other winless teams and that race for the No. 1 overall pick.
The Dolphins and Titans were joined at 0-5 this past weekend by the Los Angeles Chargers after their loss against the Denver Broncos.
While the Dolphins have a bye this weekend, the Chargers will face the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium and the Titans will face the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium.
Of the three teams at 0-5, the Chargers obviously are the big surprise considering they went into the season after back-to-back 11-win seasons, while Tennessee won three games each of the previous two seasons.
The Chargers look highly dysfunctional on offense in their first year with Mike McDaniel as their coordinator and now they're dealing with a rash of injuries that had them starting four rookies plus former Dolphins guard Cole Strange against Denver.
Working against the Chargers also is a brutal schedule. After their game at Kansas City, the Chargers will return from their bye to face the Rams, Texans (who probably are on their way to a rebound) and Baltimore, with games against the 49ers, Chiefs and Broncos over the last month.
Tennessee's bigger problem is the team just doesn't look much better than either of the previous two seasons, even if the Titans' schedule is a lot more manageable than that of either the Chargers or Dolphins. After Indy, Tennessee has a home game against Cleveland, followed by a road game against Cincinnati.
The Sporting News (Vinnie Iyer)
Analysis: The Dolphins cannot blame their continued skid on the absence of running back De'Von Achane. Another backfield star has been born, helped by Malik Willis, as Ollie Gordon II has turned 27 carries for 188 yards and 2 TDs the past two games. Gordon will help them finish an upset soon after one-possession losses to the Vikings and Bengals.
Analysis: They stay in their spot as they lost to the Bengals. The question is will they win a game.
Analysis: They're terrible and will remain that way for the duration of this season. But give them credit for fighting for first-year coach Jeff Hafley, which (unexpectedly) gets them out of the power rankings basement.
FOX Sports (Ralph Vacchiano)
Analysis: The Dolphins head into their bye week 0-5, which is exactly what everyone expected. Head coach Jeff Hafley’s defense has been OK, but they’re one of the worst offenses in the league and there isn’t a quarterback anywhere playing as poorly as Malik Willis. Bright sides? There are a few. RB Ollie Gordon has 188 yards and two TDs in two starts since they lost De’Von Achane. And on Sunday, they scored a season-high 24 points and out-gained the explosive Bengals 331 yards to 307. Want another one? When they come out of the bye, they get the Jets twice in a month span, which might be their only two chances for wins this season.
Analysis: First, the good: RB Ollie Gordon II has legitimate juice. The young playmakers out wide (plus TE Greg Dulcich) are fun to watch. LB Jacob Rodriguez is a stud who should be a front-runner for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Now, the bad: QB Malik Willis learned a hard lesson about not playing outside of his limits. Miami’s defensive weaknesses were still evident when Joe Burrow hit big plays and led steady scoring marches. The Dolphins are still winless. But for another week, they competed and didn’t make a ton of mistakes that would suggest a team headed into the abyss. That first win will come eventually.
The Athletic (Chad Graff and Josh Kendall)
Analysis: Hey, at least they fight! That’s more than can be said about the only team behind them in the rankings. The Dolphins don’t have much talent, but one week after keeping it close against the undefeated Vikings, they at least hung around with Cincinnati.
Analysis (on the biggest issue on defense, rushing the passer): It took the Dolphins until the first snap of their fourth game of the season to record their first sack; they have the NFL's second-worst sack rate. Their issues pressuring opposing quarterbacks has compounded into easy completions -- Miami ranks last in both opposing QBR and completion percentage. Going into the season, the Dolphins were thin at pass rusher behind Chop Robinson, but the 2024 first-round pick also started slow. With one of the NFL's youngest secondaries, Miami will continue to struggle against the pass until it can impact opposing QBs more consistently. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques
Pro Football Talk (Mike Florio)
Analysis: 32. Maybe Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley should have waited a year.
Sports Illustrated (Conor Orr)
Analysis: This week’s installment of Jacob Rodriguez corner: He’s leading the league in tackles but he just wants a W. How do you not love this guy?
Yahoo Sports (Frank Schwab)
Analysis: The good news for the Dolphins is they won't lose in Week 6. They have a bye. Good for the Dolphins to lose by only seven points against the Bengals on Sunday, but the true story of the game was a 28-10 deficit after three quarters. The Dolphins have trailed by at least 14 points in four of five games. There are two main goals after the bye: getting one win to avoid the 0-17 questions, and finding out if Malik Willis can be the quarterback of the future. A decision in the 2027 NFL Draft looms. Willis was 1-for-7 passing for 22 yards with a minute to go in the first half Sunday. He threw two interceptions and lost a fumble. It wasn't good enough, and garbage-time stats don't fix that. Of 32 qualified quarterbacks he's 30th in adjusted EPA (expected points added) per play and 29th in success rate. It is hard to judge Willis fairly because there's not much talent around him, but he has to prove he can elevate his teammates.

title: What to Know About New Dolphins WR Jared Wayne and the Latest Wave of Tryout Players
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are in their bye week, but the quest to upgrade their roster never takes a break.
Miami made a swap of wide receivers on their 53-man roster Tuesday when they waived Ryan Miller and claimed Jared Wayne off waivers from the Houston Texans. They also made some moves on the practice squad, signing defensive lineman Jordan Jefferson and releasing former Dallas Cowboys first-round pick Mazi Smith.
Additionally, the team continued its series of tryouts with 10 more players, including Jefferson.
It's been a long time coming for Wayne after he went undrafted in 2023. He made his NFL debut in 2024 but had appeared in only four games before playing in all five games for Houston this season, producing 65 yards on four receptions.
Wayne was waived by the Texans after they acquired Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Arizona Cardinals in a trade Sunday.
At this point, any additions are welcome. The Dolphins currently average 153.6 passing yards per game, the lowest in the NFL. Part of this issue can come from the inconsistency at the wide receiver position. Aside from Malik Washington, who has been reliable enough, the door is wide open for Wayne to become another option for Malik Willis to throw to.
Caleb Douglas showed exciting upside when he's healthy, but he missed the past three games because of an ankle injury. Chris Bell, meanwhile, was almost a non-factor in Miami's loss to Cincinnati , which could partially be his own doing thanks to some struggles creating separation.
Coming out of Pittsburgh, there was upside ahead of the 2023 Draft for Wayne, according to his draft profile. The frame is there at 6-3, 210 pounds. More than anything, though, Wayne is a strong receiver who can battle through contested catches. In addition, something that Miami might want to consider is his ability to serve as an efficient run blocker, which is a welcome attribute in an offense that can live and die on the run.
With that said, the route-running, speed, and acceleration have left a lot to be desired in his skill set, according to his draft profile and his inability to create separation could be reminiscent of Bell's struggles.
The Dolphins have held tryouts for a mix of veterans seeking another chance to get on the field and college graduates looking for an opportunity after being waived during final roster cuts August 30. Still, any chance at improvement is welcome when you're 0-5.
As mentioned at the top, Jefferson joins the Dolphins' practice squad following stops at four different teams: Jacksonville (2024 fourth-round pick), San Francisco, Cincinnati, and the Los Angeles Chargers. He's been waived by every single team he's played for, having only 12 tackles and a sack in his NFL career so far.
One name that stands out is running back Jerome Ford, who is currently in his fifth year in the NFL. He was prominent in 2023 and 2024 with Cleveland, taking over for an injured Nick Chubb before falling to the third-string role in 2025, partly due to a shoulder injury.
Defensive back Cobee Bryant could have potential based on his college resume alone. With Kansas, he showcased impressive longevity, earning three First-Team All-Big 12 Awards. He signed with Atlanta in 2025 after going undrafted, but hasn't had the opportunity to blossom in the league, recording 10 tackles and a pass deflection for the Falcons in 2025.
Tryouts are absolutely no guarantee that a player will be signed. They can simply be a shot for an unproven player to showcase their talent to an NFL coaching staff, and quarterback Jacob Clark did just that. He spent most of his college career at Missouri State, leading the Bears to their first bowl game in their first year in FBS as members of Conference USA in 2025.
Similarly, center Jaren Kump won't be vying for snaps at the position with the Dolphins anytime soon, but he did showcase flexibility at Utah by being a multi-year starter at all five positions in the trenches. He was part of a phenomenal O-line for the Utes, which also featured Cleveland's 2026 first-round pick, Spencer Fano.
Miami Hurricanes fans might recall linebacker Jahfari Harvey, who was a member of the Canes from 2019 to 2023 before transferring to SMU in 2024. He went undrafted and signed with Las Vegas in 2025 before being waived and re-signed to either the practice squad or the active roster three times in that year alone. He showcased solid pursuit and doubled as a pass rusher in college, but he hasn't had the opportunity to make the most of his versatility in the NFL just yet.
Unlike some players on this list, cornerback Dwight McGlothern didn't have trouble finding the field, appearing in 15 games for Minnesota since signing in 2024. However, he only managed a single pass deflection in 2024, and there are no listed stats for 2025. He was remarked as a ball-hawk coming out of college at Arkansas, specializing in zone coverage but being weak against the run.
Linebacker Jeremiah Moon signed with Baltimore as an undrafted free agent in 2022 before being waived, then signing with both Pittsburgh and Carolina not once, but twice from 2024 to 2026. All in all, he's appeared in 25 games and has recorded 31 tackles and two forced fumbles. Strength is his specialty in the NFL, as it was in college at Florida, but if he were to find a home with Miami, it might be for punt coverage, as it was something he was known to do with the Gators.
Likewise, tight end Messiah Swinson's list of NFL teams since 2024 is a bit convoluted, but the bottom line is that he hasn't had an opportunity to record playing time with Green Bay, Carolina, San Francisco, Arizona, or Cleveland. He was a solid target in the red zone at Arizona State, but of all the players on this list, he might have the least chance of landing a spot on Miami, almost solely due to a lack of film and a lack of need at the position.
Offensive tackle Da'Metrius Weatherspoon was a recent release from New England's practice squad. This followed a stellar season for Syracuse in 2025, mainly served as a right tackle but did start one game at left guard. He only allowed four sacks and committed three penalties in 817 snaps, and was the highest-rated player on the Orange's offense, with a 76.5 rating, according to Pro Football Focus.

title: Revisiting the Jonathan Greenard Trade Five Weeks into the Season (Did the Vikings Come Out on Top?)
full_text:
The Vikings reluctantly traded star pass-rusher Jonathan Greenard ahead of the 2026 NFL Draft, ending a brief two-year stint in Minnesota. It was a complicated trade that interim general manager Rob Brzezinski had said "was not something we're jumping around excitedly about." And while the Vikings weren't exactly thrilled to make the trade initially, have they come around since?
After Greenard asked for a raise the Vikings were unwilling to meet, they dealt him to Philadelphia for a 2026 third-round pick and a 2027 third-rounder this spring. What initially seemed like a light haul for one of their best defensive players, the deal--at least right now--looks like it could lean in Minnesota's favor.
Let's start with Greenard, who, dating back to last season has struggled to just stay on the field. After missing five games in 2025 with Minnesota, Greenard has only been able to suit up twice this season in Philly, notching just one tackle and zero sacks in those contests. So while his ability has rarely been called into question, his availability entering his thirties is now something to monitor.
Greenard has now had three separate injuries—a shoulder, a pec and an ankle, that have forced him to miss time, and it's fair to wonder if he'll reach the same heights as before. After an unfortunate start, it already looks like the Eagles may be looking towards 2027 for their return on investment.
The Vikings, on the other hand, certainly haven't been disappointed with Greenard's replacement, as Dallas Turner leads the team in sacks with 5.5. The 23-year-old is a budding star, and Minnesota certainly has their edge of the future. And although Turner's future is crystal clear, Jakobe Thomas', whom the Vikings selected with their first pick from the Greenard trade, is much more nebulous.
Minnesota nabbed the safety with the 98th overall pick, and is surely a developmental project for the Vikings. After missing much of the preseason with a back injury, Thomas has now been inactive for every game of the 2026 season so far.
Despite early concerns at safety with the struggles of Harrison Smith and Joshua Metellus, the Vikings seem keen on leaving their third-round pick on the bench. Undrafted free agent Jacob Thomas is already ahead on the depth chart. While Jakobe's story won't be written in 2026 alone, it's clear the safety has some growing to do.
The Vikings still have another third-round pick in 2027 coming their way, so the winner of the trade may not be clear for some time. But as it stands right now, neither team is probably too thrilled with their acquisitions so far.
The Eagles made Greenard a very rich man with a new $100 million deal, and have yet to see much of him. Meanwhile, the Vikings have gotten great production from Turner, but Thomas' impact is far from being recognized.
Ultimately, while the Vikings never wanted to deal Greenard in the first place, it did pave the way for Turner to be unleashed. Coupled with Greenard's new price tag and injuries, most people in the building are probably pretty happy despite the limited rookie production so far.

title: Jalen Redmond's Breakout Is Leaving Vikings With an Interesting Conundrum
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings moved on from veterans Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave this offseason and drafted two players in the 2026 NFL Draft to replace them. The team used a first-round pick on Caleb Banks and a third-round pick on Domonique Orange to fill those gaps heading into this season.
The forgotten man in that equation was Jalen Redmond. A 27-year-old defensive lineman in his third NFL season. He has earned a huge role with the Vikings, as evidenced by his snap counts increasing with every passing year.
Now, his impact on Minnesota's defensive line can't be ignored. He has a Pro Football Focus grade of 76.6 through the Vikings' first five games, registering nine quarterback pressures, 15 combined tackles, two pass deflections, and one forced fumble in 236 defensive snaps.
Typically, seeing a player like Redmond thrive in Minnesota's defense wouldn't be a problem. However, he is a restricted free agent after this year and should be in line for a healthy increase in pay for 2027 and beyond.
Redmond's price tag could be around $15 million per year based on the salaries earned by players like Broncos defender D.J. Jones and the Colts' Grover Stewart.
While that doesn't sound like a lot of money, the Vikings are expected to have about $35 million of cap space next season and have a long list of players like Andrew Van Ginklel, T.J. Hockenson, Blake Cashman, Isaiah Rodgers, and more who need to be re-signed.
The Vikings still have salary cap wizard Rob Brzezinski in the front office, so it will be interesting to see what kind of magic he can work with the team's contracts during the offseason, but at least for now, it looks like keeping Redmond around could be a challenge.
Considering Redmond's youth and ability, he will be a player who Minnesota wants to keep around. Putting him on the defensive line with Banks and Orange sounds like a great recipe for the future of the Vikings' defensive line, but the team will need to figure out a way to make that happen by navigating the salary cap.
Redmond is currently the top-graded defensive tackle against the run in the NFL, according to PFF , and would be a great player to have on the defensive line in the future, especially if Banks and Orange can step into a starting role for the Purple and Gold when they are ready.

title: One Specific Week 6 Matchup Should Have Vikings' Attention During Their Bye
full_text:
The Vikings may have their bye week in Week 6, but that doesn't mean there aren't great reasons to watch some of this weekend's games . While the Purple and Gold get rest and their banged-up players get some much-needed time to heal, one game in particular should have fans' attention.
Of course, divisional matchups are always interesting and will have a big impact on the season. Games like the Bears vs. the Falcons and the Cowboys vs. the Packers on Sunday Night Football will be interesting, but an AFC matchup might be more deserving of the Vikings' attention.
At noon on Sunday, the Titans face off against the Colts in a game that may seem irrelevant in the scope of the current season, but Vikings fans have good reason to pay close attention to the AFC South showdown.
The biggest reason to keep tabs on the aforementioned AFC South showdown is that the Vikings play the Colts in Week 7. That game at U.S. Bank Stadium will not only put the Purple and Gold's undefeated record on the line as they come out of their bye, but it will also feature former Vikings quarterback Daniel Jones under center for the opposition.
Since leaving Minnesota, Jones has gone 10-8 while completing 65.9% of passes for 4,122 passing yards and 22 touchdowns to 12 interceptions, with a 91.8 passer rating. He's also picked up 189 rushing yards and six more scores on 59 carries.
Getting a good look at Jones and Indianapolis star running back Jonathan Taylor (504 total yards from scrimmage and six TDs on 114 touches) will give Minnesota a sense of what to expect next week. That said, the Vikings also have plenty of reason to pay attention to the Titans on Sunday afternoon.
Recently, SKOR North 's Judd Zulgad shared an interesting thought : the Vikings' offense desperately needs running back help behind Aaron Jones Sr., so Zulgad pitches Titans RB Tony Pollard as a potential target.
The Titans are 0-5 and have not been competitive this season. It may not take more than a mid-round draft pick to land Pollard if Tennessee decides to prepare for the future and throw in the towel this season. Meanwhile, he could be a great asset for Minnesota.
Pollard is 29 years old and has been one of the only solid parts of the Titans' roster this year.
Through five games this season, he has 68 carries for 273 yards and a touchdown, while adding eight catches for 24 yards. His four yards per carry is interesting considering how bad Tennessee has been this year. Not only that, but he has a Pro Football Focus grade of 71 for the year , placing him 12th out of 44 qualifying running backs.
Aaron Jones won't be the Vikings' starter forever. Pairing Pollard with Jordan Mason for the future makes a lot of sense and would provide more future stability while solidifying the backfield depth this season.
It will be interesting to see whether Minnesota inquires about Pollard's potential availability before the Nov. 10 trade deadline, especially if the losses keep piling up for the Titans. Let's see if the possibility of a Vikings-Titans trade becomes more likely after Sunday.

title: Potential Ben Bredeson Trade Makes Too Much Sense for Vikings to Ignore
full_text:
As the bye week continues, Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley is likely weighing the various avenues he can take to address his team's remaining roster problems. Specifically, the offensive ones. Whether it's more depth at wide receiver or help in the backfield, the Vikings clearly need help to unlock more firepower after averaging 21.8 points (T-21st) and 283 total yards (27th) per game through five weeks.
The left side of the offensive line is also a concern after the Vikings lost tackle Christian Darrisaw to concussion protocol, while guard Donovan Jackson's season is over due to a torn meniscus . Former undrafted blocker Joe Huber has been solid but nothing special filling in for Jackson so far; no one would blame Teasley & Co. for wanting more LG depth—if not someone who'd even improve the starting lineup.
That's why veteran guard Ben Bredeson could be on the Vikings' radar heading into the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline. With the Buccaneers heading towards seller's territory as they enter Week 6 with a 1-4 record, it makes sense for Teasley to give Tampa Bay GM Jason Licht a call.
If the last name sounds familiar, it's because the Buccaneers' blocker is the elder brother of Vikings rookie fullback Max Bredeson. Although a family reunion would certainly be heartwarming, a potential trade for the former 2020 fourth-rounder isn't just about reuniting the brothers or improving the locker room's already-good vibes.
After all, the elder Bredeson boasts the kind of experience Minnesota's O-line could use at the moment. The 28-year-old gap-opener has played 78 games (58 starts) across his time with the Buccaneers, Giants, and Ravens, as well as a trio of postseason appearances. Although he's played all three interior positions, most of Bredeson's snaps have come at left guard , where he's played 2,960 compared with 586 at center and 487 on the right side, per Pro Football Focus .
This is about adding LG depth, but that versatility could come in handy as injuries pile up later in the season.
Bredeson's individual stats won't blow anyone away, but he's still been a reliable asset on a struggling Bucs team this season. According to Pro Football Focus , his 61.2 run-block grade is tied for the second-best effort of his career , while his 62.9 pass-block grade is his third-best. For comparison, Huber owns grades of 60.5 and 46.5, respectively.
Jackson was arguably the Vikings' best offensive lineman before his injury, and while he's expected to make a full recovery, it isn't guaranteed that he'll pick up where he left off. He still needs to recover and go through rehab before proving himself all over again throughout the offseason, which is why having another capable LG around—even if you include Huber—would be a good idea.
Fortunately, Bredeson would be more than an average deadline rental that Minnesota would need to re-sign at season's end. The former Michigan Wolverine is under contract for the 2027 season with an affordable $8.2 million cap hit , according to Spotrac . And even if he proves to be a poor fit, the Vikings can designate him for a post-June 1 release, saving $7 million in cap space while leaving dead money in 2027 ($1.2 million) and 2028 ($2.5 million).
A trade also likely wouldn't cost Teasley too much draft capital. Bleacher Report' s Alex Kay projects the Vikings acquiring Bredeson and a 2027 seventh-rounder for a fifth-round pick in April's draft. While I don't think the Buccaneers would want to send any picks back if they're blowing it up, I could see the Vikings needing to give up a 2027 fourth- or fifth-rounder, along with one from the sixth or seventh round in 2028.
Assuming the Buccaneers keep losing, proven veterans like Bredeson will attract attention from playoff contenders. The Vikings should be in that conversation, especially since Jackson's year is done, giving them every reason to call the Bucs sooner rather than later.
