title: Saints vs. Vikings: The Good, Bad and Ugly From New Orleans' 23-13 Loss
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' struggles continued Sunday as they fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings inside the Caesars Superdome.
The defeat dropped New Orleans to 1-4 for the second consecutive season, further exposing the growing problems facing second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a team that continues to take steps backward .
Here is the Good, Bad and Ugly from the Saints' 23-13 loss to the Vikings.
In one of the few bright spots in the loss to the Vikings, Saints 2nd year safety Jonas Sanker provided a game-changing spark by returning a fumble 88 yards for a touchdown to tie the game at 13-13 late in the second quarter.
Sanker's touchdown demonstrated that New Orleans still has young players capable of making an impact despite a disappointing 1-4 start, though Daniel Carlson subsequently missed the go-ahead extra point.
Fumble 🗣️ Jonas Sanker recovers and takes it to the end zone to tie it up! @MINvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/W52Ypr6gtT
The second-year defensive back has been tasked with helping rebuild a Saints defense that has undergone significant turnover, delivering an impressive defensive scoring play against Minnesota's undefeated squad.
Ultimately, the Saints' offense failed to capitalize on the momentum, leaving the defense with little margin for error as New Orleans dropped its fourth game of the season.
Shough has been the Saints’ best player throughout the season as he, along with a few others, is the bright spot on what is a bad football team at the moment and if it weren’t for him this season would be a complete disaster.
However, his performance was not good enough for New Orleans to win this game.
Shough had his worst game of the season, completing 16 of his 25 passes for only 96 yards and two interceptions. A lot of his struggles could be placed on the Vikings’ defense and their blitz packages, which present a lot of looks that could deceive a quarterback and his offensive line.
"It was obviously very difficult," Shough said of going up against Minnesota’s defense. "They presented a lot of looks. That's what they're extremely good at. I felt like we were ready for all those looks. We just didn't execute in some of those moments, and now we're second and 20, or third and 15, and — I mean, you're not — those odds are not really in your favor for those situations.
"And we got to be in those third-and-six, third-and-five, third-and-three ranges, where we can convert and dictate tempo. We had a couple good drives and moments, but I don't care who we're playing, we got to be better there. And especially against that team, they're really well coached, really played really well."
While the Saints’ defense allowed a putrid Minnesota offense to put up its best numbers of the season, the most concerning aspect of Sunday's defeat occurred off the field.
The game served as a stark reminder that the Caesars Superdome no longer offers the formidable environment it was once famous for.
Historically, New Orleans boasted one of the premier home-field advantages in the NFL, where deafening crowd noise and an unyielding Saints team made life miserable for visiting opponents.
That distinct edge appears to have vanished.
The Saints have lost all of their four home games this year (including preseason), extending a troubling pattern that began after former head coach Sean Payton left the team following the 2021 campaign.
Since Payton's departure, New Orleans has posted a sub-.500 record of 15-21 at home, managing just a single winning season in the Superdome (5-3 in 2023).
The situation has grown even more dire recently, as the Saints have dropped 14 of their last 17 home contests since the start of 2024.
Yet, the venue's atmosphere on Sunday was perhaps just as unsettling as the loss itself.
A massive contingent of traveling Vikings supporters made their presence felt, filling the Superdome with loud, distinct "Skol" chants.
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
For an organization that built its reputation on creating a hostile environment for opponents, watching opposing fans dominate sections of the stadium underscored the team's ongoing decline.
Understandably, persistent losing eventually takes a toll on crowd enthusiasm and game-day attendance.
With little evidence of progress on the field, fan frustration continues to mount alongside the team's home struggles.
Reestablishing a true home-field advantage will require more than past glory or fan loyalty.
It must be reclaimed by winning football games.
Until Moore and the Saints deliver better results in front of their home crowd, visiting teams and their fans will continue to feel right at home in New Orleans.

title: Saints-Vikings Game Day Primer: Injuries, Key Stats and Players to Watch
full_text:
Seeking to recover from a humiliating defeat to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night, the New Orleans Saints (1-3) return to the Caesars Superdome this Sunday for a Week 5 clash with the undefeated Minnesota Vikings (4-0).
Beyond the action on the field, Sunday's contest carries extra weight as New Orleans pays tribute to an iconic figure in team history. Legendary former quarterback Drew Brees —a recently enshrined Hall of Famer who brought the city its first Super Bowl title and set multiple NFL passing records across 15 memorable seasons—will be formally inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor.
This special induction elevates the stakes for second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a Saints squad eager to secure its initial home win of the campaign. Standing in their path is a formidable Minnesota roster that remains unblemished, anchored by a suffocating defense yielding a league-best 12.8 points per game.
Below is a complete preview and key details for today's matchup.

title: Giants Draw Penalty-Light Crew for Saints Game, but History Gives Pause
full_text:
John Harbaugh quickly improved the New York Giants ’ preparation, situational awareness, aggression, and win-loss record . Still, he needed a little more time to fix their penalty problem.
Well, it looks like he's starting to solve that Rubik’s Cube, too. The Giants have now accumulated fewer than 50 penalty yards in back-to-back games, something they couldn’t do last season.
Under their new head coach, Big Blue has gone from a frequent offender toward the top half of the league. The referee report suggests that the positive trend may continue in Week 6.
Lead official Alex Kemp and his crew will work Sunday afternoon’s home matchup versus the New Orleans Saints, according to Football Zebras . Kemp’s crew has issued just 54 penalties for 451 yards, ranking second and fifth among all crews this season.
Kemp looks like an excellent draw on paper, but the Giants haven’t seen him in a while. And when they did, it was not pretty.
During the 2024 season opener, New York got hit with nine penalties for a whopping 95 yards in a 28-6 loss against Sam Darnold and the Minnesota Vikings. Adding more concern, Kemp’s penalty total spiked in last Sunday’s AFC South clash between the Houston Texans and Tennessee Titans.
The Titans, at home, were assessed 83 penalty yards, and the visiting Texans were flagged 11 times for 95 yards. This is an anomaly for 2026, though. The Giants and their fans can only hope that Kemp and company revert to their usual modest count.
Kemp’s crew has a couple of new faces, including side judge Jim Quirk and replay assistant Kris Raper.
They join umpire Brandon Ellison, down judge Mike Carr, line judge Rusty Baynes, field judge Sean Petty, and back judge Scott Helverson. Julie Johnson, previously the crew’s replay assistant, is now the replay official.
The Giants must focus on what they can control, and they have been doing an excellent job at that lately. Their 301 penalty yards-against ranks 18th in the NFL, a clear sign of improvement.
There is still plenty to fix in that area, but this squad is playing with much more discipline over the last couple of games. The upcoming meeting with New Orleans will be a good test to see how much the Giants have truly changed.
Last season against the Saints, New York blew a 14-3 lead, committed a nauseating five turnovers, and racked up eight penalties for 95 yards in a 26-14 loss in the Caesars Superdome.
Harbaugh aims to change that result this time around.

title: Giants’ Roster Move Hints at Possible Plan for Running Backs Against the Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants have elevated outside linebacker Trace Ford from their practice squad in their only move before Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints.
By elevating only Ford, who has played 19 defensive snaps and 47 special teams snaps in two games this season and has been elevated twice, the Giants are notably rolling with just four receivers (Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, and Charlie Jones) against the Saints.
That could mean the Giants plan to have all four of their running backs (Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr., Najee Harris, and Devin Singletary) active for this week’s game.
Singletary has been a healthy scratch for the last three weeks. But given his ability to contribute on special teams and questions about whether Skattebo, the team’s lead back, could see a reduced role because of his fumbling issue, this could be how the Giants want to approach their personnel.
Head coach John Harbaugh was asked Friday where he draws the line between sticking with a struggling player and making a change.
“I don’t know that there is really a rule for it. It’s case-by-case. It depends on your options. It depends on what you’re talking about,” he said.
“There are also levels of establishment in players and things like that. Some things are more up in the air at positions, and some things are more established. It’s just probably more case-by-case.”
Skattebo, now in his second season, has 294 rushing yards, which ranks 16th among running backs. But he’s averaging 0.72 yards before contact, which ranks 35th of 41 qualifying running backs, while his 2.91 yards after contact per carry ranks 20th.
The most glaring number working against Skattebo is his fumble total: three so far, with one lost. The three fumbles rank second among the league’s running backs, behind Buffalo’s James Cook, who has four.
When asked specifically whether there is a point where accountability comes into play for the running backs, Harbaugh said, “Of course. Yes, there is a point.”

title: Giants’ O-Line Is Trending Up, but the Run Game and Tackle Injuries Are Red Flags
full_text:
For most of the first five weeks of the 2026 NFL season, the New York Giants ’ offensive line has rarely been a source of fan complaints.
The team’s handful of offseason investments in the group seem to have extended its 2025 success and paid early dividends, with New York’s unit ranking eighth in the league in pass-blocking efficiency after finishing in the top three a year ago.
Even with the unexpected change at quarterback from the injured Jaxson Dart to Jameis Winston, the Giants have put together a few strong offensive outings that are among the catalysts for their 3-1-1 start, which puts them atop the NFC East standings through five games for the first time since 2009.
However, the old injury issue that used to mar the offensive line almost every year is starting to rear its ugly head again. In particular, the bookend tackles, Andrew Thomas (groin) and Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), either played through or had to leave their Week 5 matchup against the Washington Commanders because of ailments.
Both players’ statuses raise concerns as the Giants prepare for their next home game against the New Orleans Saints, yet the unit still earned a three-spot jump to No. 17 in PFF’s latest offensive line rankings .
PFF elevated the Giants’ offensive line mainly because of the recent switch from John Michael Schmitz to Bryan Hudson at starting center.
The Giants tried to be patient with Schmitz, but the fourth-year player hasn’t lived up to his second-round draft status. Injuries forced him to miss 10 games in his first three seasons with the team, and his inability to wrestle with bigger defensive tackles has dented his overall blocking.
John Harbaugh’s decision to move Hudson to the starting middle has brought back some promising returns. The former undrafted free agent has been stellar in his first 102 snaps, allowing just one pressure and being a serviceable blocker in the run game.
While it is good to see improvement at one position along the offensive front, it doesn’t cure the two glaring issues that have started to plague the Giants’ success: key injuries and a failure to produce solid protection for the rushing attack.
The Giants have posted more than 100 yards on the ground in three of their first five games, but the bully-ball prowess they sought to terrorize opposing defenses just hasn’t made a huge difference.
Harbaugh made sure to bring over his beloved fullback, Patrick Ricard, from Baltimore to help the cause and provide an extra 300-pound force to open up rushing lanes for Cam Skattebo and company, and the addition has been serviceable.
Ricard can’t affect the first line of protection, though. That comes from the three interior linemen (Jon Runyan, Schmitz before he was benched, and rookie Francis Mauigoa), and entering Week 6, all three are sitting near the basement of the Giants’ run-blocking grades and have been prone to committing some of the team’s penalties on those plays.
As their efforts haven't held up week to week, New York’s interior rushing efficiency has started to plummet toward the bottom half of the league. The Giants rank 25th in average yards per rush up the middle (3.02) and barely tread above 4 yards per attempt between the guard spots.
Not all of the rushing woes belong to the offensive line, either. The backfield also deserves some blame for poor ball protection that has yielded five fumbles in as many games, including the most recent by Skattebo in overtime against the Commanders, which nearly gave the Giants a crushing divisional loss.
Still, the protection up front has to improve if the Giants want to rely more on their physical ground game at a higher clip than the 3.7 yards per carry the team is averaging overall.
The Giants will also need to monitor how things progress with Thomas and Eluemunor, since the two veteran tackles are arguably the best pass blockers the team has had in recent years.
Repairing what has been a weak run game is hard enough. Losing one or both of those pieces for this Sunday’s game against the Saints could make for an even tougher afternoon for Big Blue’s inconsistent offense.

title: Giants Scouting Report: How to Attack the Saints’ Struggling Defense
full_text:
Even while dealing with the weather elements, the New York Giants offense has found success passing the ball over the past couple of weeks as everyone settles into the Jameis Winston experience.
While the rushing attack hasn’t exactly been what the team was hoping for, or what fans believed they were getting when John Harbaugh put this squad together, a 3-1-1 record has to be attributed to the way this offense has rallied and performed under pressure.
Now the Giants face the New Orleans defense, which has been vulnerable to teams running the ball and giving up points. This could be another great opportunity for them to improve their record.
Let’s break down the Saints’ defense.
Under defensive coordinator Brandon Staley, the Saints run a modern odd-front hybrid defense that can shift from 3-4 to 3-3, 4-2 and 2-4 looks based on personnel.
Those differences usually depend heavily on run or pass downs, or on personnel that suggest run or pass. They rely on strong, explosive defensive linemen up front to occupy double teams and allow second-level defenders to attack downhill.
They also need second-level defenders who can run-fit and troubleshoot quickly to make plays.
The Saints’ rushing defense ranks near the bottom of the league. Their 148.8 yards per game allowed ranks 30th, and their 4.86 yards per carry allowed ranks 26th.
Both numbers scream to run the ball against this team to control the clock and maximize opportunities to win the game, while keeping possession away from their offense.
When odd-front defenses struggle with run fits, it usually leads to inflated rushing totals for opponents.
Bryan Bresee is the Saints’ best defensive lineman, based primarily on his versatility across the line.
He can play interior as a pass-rushing nose guard, or defensive end in an odd front.
He is comfortable as an interior lineman taking on double teams, and he can take advantage of 1-on-1 matchups.
It will be important for the Giants not only to know where he is, but to have a plan for stopping him on Sunday.
The Saints’ passing defense ranks 11th, but that’s a bit of fool’s gold. The ranking is so high because teams have run the ball so effectively against them that they haven’t needed to pass.
That is evident in the Saints’ yards per attempt allowed: 7.46, which ranks 23rd. They don’t hold rushing offenses down enough to force opponents to pass.
But when opponents have passed, they have found a lot of success. That’s surprising, since the Saints regularly play five defensive backs in their secondary.
Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry is the Saints’ best defensive back. He typically mans the boundary side in coverage. He does a great job using press technique consistently to disrupt receivers’ releases off the line of scrimmage.
He is also consistent in his ability to mirror on perimeter routes and force quarterbacks to throw tight-window completions.
The Giants should be able to scheme around McKinstry based on where he normally lines up, then exploit the other coverage players who have struggled this year.
Linebacker Kaden Elliss has missed multiple practices and has been ruled out with a calf injury. His absence makes the defense even more susceptible to rushing offenses.
Edge rusher Anfernee Jennings remains out with knee issues. Meanwhile, defensive linemen Christian Miller and Davon Godchaux are dealing with weekly illnesses and soft-tissue injuries as they prepare for the game ahead.
Safety Julian Blackmon has been limited in practice with a shoulder injury. Rookie safety Lorenzo Styles Jr. has also been limited in practice and is questionable for the game with calf and knee injuries.
The Giants have to run the ball. They must make the Saints commit more bodies to the line of scrimmage than they want to, so they can take advantage of their 1-on-1 matchups in the passing game with Nabers, Likely, and Malachi Fields, who has been quietly gaining more traction through the first five games.
Yes, they want the rushing attack to get on track, and this seems to be the team to do it against. But they don’t want to sacrifice what should be easy points and a simple ability to move the ball just to get a part of their offense working that hasn’t been at its best this season.
If the Giants can run the ball effectively, it will open up a legitimate play-action game, where they should find receivers running wide open at the intermediate level and possibly even connecting on some deep routes.

title: Giants Draft Watch: Four College Prospects to Track in Week 7
full_text:
As the New York Giants (3-1-1) prepare for a Week 6 matchup with the New Orleans Saints (1-4) at MetLife Stadium, several Big Blue scouts will be keeping close watch on the Week 7 college football slate.
New York is eyeing potential targets as they make their cases for selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. The team’s biggest needs remain along both its offensive and defensive lines.
Head coach John Harbaugh and his staff also appear to want to add talent in the defensive backfield.
In that regard, here are four players the Giants may keep a close eye on this weekend.
Widely considered one of the most pro-ready offensive line prospects in the 2027 draft class, Bobo is expected to use his wealth of football knowledge to become an immediate impact player.
With John Michael Schmitz likely heading to free agency after being replaced in the starting lineup by Bryan Hudson, the 6-foot-5, 305-pound Bulldogs center could be an intriguing option for New York.
Though Hudson has performed well to date, he is also slated to become an exclusive-rights free agent at season’s end. If the Giants want a more permanent option, Bobo should be on their radar.
The son of Georgia offensive coordinator Mike Bobo, the 22-year-old has been well schooled in quickly recognizing pre-snap defensive alignments and coordinating his fellow linemen.
Having added significant muscle during his tenure in Athens, Georgia, Bobo has become a formidable force in both pass protection and run blocking.
In fact, the Georgia native’s discipline, character and outstanding play have recently earned him a spot on the 2026 Rotary Lombardi Award Midseason Watch List.
If Georgia has success moving the ball against Auburn’s defense in Week 7, Bobo will need to play an integral role in the offense.
With his blend of size and speed, Moten is expected to bring unique potential to the interior of an NFL defensive line. Projected best as a 3-technique rotational tackle, the Hurricanes’ standout has been linked to the Giants by several draft analysts.
Although an early-season shoulder scare and a Week 6 bye have limited him to just two games played, the 6-foot-3, 325-pounder has four total tackles, one sack and one forced fumble this season.
Moten could be a day-one contributor for the Giants based on his ability to attack the inside on pass defense.
Though he could use a bit of work on his anchor and hand placement against the run, his strength and aggressiveness should be on full display this week against Florida State’s offense.
If the Giants want to add a speedy, lengthy cornerback with noteworthy upside in man coverage, Hill is a player to watch. The 6-foot-2, 190-pound defensive back has already become a disruptive force in the Wolverines’ defense, collecting 25 total tackles and one interception through five games this season.
Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is known for his penchant for sticky, press-man coverage. In fact, the Giants lead the league in Cover-0 usage at 11%. Hill’s straight-line speed lets him succeed vertically.
He is also adept at diagnosing run plays at the snap, giving him a chance to succeed downhill. Given the Giants’ need for both depth and versatility in the defensive backfield, they may find it beneficial to scout Hill as either a Day 2 or Day 3 prospect during this weekend’s game against Penn State.
While Alabama’s program has frequently been described as an assembly line for NFL-ready talent, Hubbard is a player worthy of such praise.
At 6-foot-2 and 217 pounds, Hubbard can play as a hybrid safety-linebacker in New York’s defensive backfield. Through the first six games of the season, he has collected 26 total tackles, two interceptions and one forced fumble.
At the pro level, Hubbard projects as a top-flight downhill run defender who can tackle from the box. He also possesses the speed and on-field savvy to defend tight ends in coverage.
Should the Giants continue their upward trend of deploying the blitz at a high rate, Hubbard should get more than a passing look from Big Blue’s scouting contingent, especially against a high-powered Tennessee offense in Week 7.

title: Giants Mailbag: Run Game Woes, Skattebo’s Fumbles, Deonte Banks’ Contract and More
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
Who is this man that is always with the head coach? Not just this year but previous years too. And what is his role? #askPTrain pic.twitter.com/Ea2LCyjtl1
That's Jerry Meade, who is in charge of the team's security operations.
From Ross McLaren : Hi, is the run game as bad as it looks? How do the Giants make it better, and can Skattebo be a legit number one back?
Ross, I think it’s a combination of factors, starting with run blocking, which PFF ranks.
The lack of explosive runs is another problem. I don’t think the Giants have leaned heavily on players with that kind of explosiveness for those plays.
I suspect the loss of Jaxson Dart, who, as we know, is a running quarterback, contributed to the issue, as defenses no longer have to account for the quarterback as a potential running threat.
In Week 1 with Dart, the Giants rushed for 165 yards. Since he’s been out of the lineup, they’ve averaged 95 rushing yards per game.
In that first game with Dart, they had a season-best 4.5 yards per carry. Since then, the closest they’ve come was Week 3 against Tennessee, when they averaged 4.2 yards per carry.
Ball security issues haven’t helped either, and neither has their first-down rushing efficiency. Per NFL+, they have a -0.16 EPA (Expected Points Added) on first-down runs, which ranks 23rd in the league. They are also averaging 3.3 yards per carry on first downs.
So yes, the running game has been as bad as it’s looked, and to improve it, they have to address where it’s lacking.
As for Skattebo being an RB1, that is his current role on the team, though I wouldn’t be surprised if we see Najee Harris take on more rushing snaps, given Skattebo’s ball-security issues.
From Kevin C. (via email): Harbaugh’s postgame comments about Skattebo’s fumble in Washington were infuriating: “He’ll learn from that” and “He’s got to be better next time.”
Four fumbles in five games! What makes anyone think it won’t continue? The inexcusable turnover Sunday cost the Giants a win. When will Harbaugh do something about it? After five fumbles, six, 10?
I wonder if you agree that it’s time to bench Skattebo. I think he should be inactive against New Orleans. They have three other running backs who are less likely to fumble and have been equally ineffective rushing for yardage. Time for a change, right?
Kevin, absolutely not, just as I don’t agree with the decision to remove Tyrone Tracy from the offense in favor of Najee Harris, whom I view as a runner similar to Skattebo.
I get the frustration you’re feeling, but a good coach gets to the root of the problem and fixes it. If the coach can’t fix it, then you make a move.
Players and coaches say every turnover has its own story. Maybe, but look for a recurring thread and get to the bottom of it. Dive into the film and see if there is a small gap between the ball and Skattebo’s body (which I wrote about in this article ) and work with him to fix it.
Also drill it into his head that it’s okay to call it a day every so often, instead of fighting for an extra yard or two which puts the ball at risk of being punched out.
From James L. McMahan Jr. : What are your feelings on how Deonte Banks is playing this year?
Hi, James. Banks has been playing extremely well. I’ve always said that he had loads of talent and that he was his own worst enemy.
I said that if he stopped beating himself up when something went wrong and came back swinging, he would live up to his billing. He’s proving me correct this season, and I’m glad for him.
I get that he was frustrated last season and felt like he was spinning his wheels, but not everything in life goes according to expectations, and you either sink or swim.
From Kris Kauffeld : Tae Banks is off to a good start this year. It’s the last year of his contract. Can the Giants give him a new contract during the season, and if so, should they open those conversations?
What’s good, Kris? Can the Giants give Banks a new contract during the season? Yes. They can give anyone an extension. I think you meant to ask whether they should give him a new contract right now.
My answer is no, for two reasons.
First, if I’m Banks, I play out the rest of the season and keep building a case for a nice payday. Maybe I have my agent find out what the Giants might be thinking, and then I use that as a base. But no way do I take a contract extension now, given how the season has gone so far.
Second, from the Giants’ perspective, they have $9.86 million in remaining cap space to get them through the rest of the season. They have already cut into all the big-money contracts on the roster to free up cap space, except for cornerback Paulson Adebo, whom I suspect they’ll cut after this year.
Remember, if they extend a player, the signing bonus proration starts the year it was signed unless both sides agree to defer, and that’s rare.
Financially speaking, I don’t see how it’s possible unless they say, “Trade Kayvon Thibodeaux and use those savings for a Banks extension.” And I don’t see that happening either.
From Joe G. (via email): Please explain the logic of some members of the press who are calling for the Giants to trade Thibodeaux. Trading him when two of your other pass rushers are out is just plain foolish. The Giants are not losing with him. Yet the press is foolishly calling for his trade. Where is the logic?
Joe, if you want my opinion on the matter — I am not going to speak for anyone else — there are two potential reasons.
First, his pass-rush productivity hasn’t been very good. That said, he makes a lot of little plays that don’t register on the stat sheet, and I think that gets overlooked.
Second, if Thibodeaux isn’t in the long-term plans and you can get something for him that you can use next year to replenish what you don’t have, why not make the move?
If he walks away in free agency, and I wouldn’t be shocked if he does, there is no guarantee you get a decent comp pick back to use the following year.
And if you feel good about Carter and Reese right now and think you can get something out of Jihad Ward on the pass rush this year, then maybe it’s not as silly an idea as it was earlier.
Personally, I don’t think a trade happens. Any team that trades for him is, in essence, getting a half-season rental unless it signs him to an extension.
And regarding your statement that “the Giants are not losing with him,” that doesn’t hold water. They weren’t losing with John Michael Schmitz at center, and yet they still made the switch. Since when is it wrong to make a lineup change when the opportunity is there and the situation warrants it?
From Pat L. (via email): Fresh off watching the Giants-Commanders game, these Giants feel different. A year ago this would have been a loss. Even after Zvada’s missed field goal attempt and Skattebo’s fumble, the Giants pulled out a tie. What do you attribute the change to?
Coaching. Pure and simple. Did you catch the adjustments they made? There’s been no more of this: “We’ll stick with the game plan and hope it works out.”
This staff is far more proactive than I recall previous ones being, and it’s paying off. Do you think they come back from a 14-point deficit in years past? I don’t.
Also, we have to credit Washington’s poor clock management at the end there. It almost reminded me of “The Fumble” from years ago, when all the Giants had to do was fall on the ball to seal the deal against the Eagles, and they got cute. Only thing is that instead of the Giants getting cute, this time it was their opponent.

How do double-digit wins and a postseason berth, possibly as the division winner, sound? Let’s break this down.

title: Isaiah Likely Feels at Home in Giants’ Offense, and His Chemistry With Jameis Winston Is Growing
full_text:
While he may be the metaphorical “new kid on the block,” New York Giants tight end Isaiah Likely already feels at home in Big Blue’s offense.
Through the first five games of the season, the five-year veteran has caught 33 passes for 284 yards and four touchdowns. In the process, he has established himself as New York’s top option at the position.
Still, the road to Likely’s present success has not been entirely well-paved. After losing incumbent starting quarterback Jaxson Dart to a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, the Cambridge, Massachusetts, native has toiled to develop similar chemistry with current starter Jameis Winston .
Despite some initial growing pains, the pair appears to have finally forged a productive gridiron relationship.
In his best statistical outing of the season, Likely logged 11 catches for 94 yards and two touchdowns during New York’s Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders.
He became the first Giants tight end in franchise history with nine or more receptions and two or more receiving touchdowns in a single game.
Most importantly, Likely has become a much-needed, reliable target for Winston in short-yardage situations. Fortunately for the Giants, the Likely-Winston duo appears to be just getting started.
“I feel like we’re getting there day in and day out,” Likely said of his working relationship with Winston. “I mean, obviously, you’re never going to be perfect. But I feel like me, Jameis, and the whole offense as a whole are really just taking the right trajectory right now.”
Since joining the Giants as a free agent this offseason, Likely has been a key factor in coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense.
Although the veteran offensive coordinator is known for his methodical, run-centric, motion-based offense, the 6-foot-4, 245-pounder has been a highly targeted weapon in the passing game. Likely blends a capable route-running skill set with strong contested-catch ability, especially when high-pointing the ball.
For a player his size, he shows above-average acceleration, which often translates to notable yards after the catch. He can succeed in open-field coverage, and he can also be used on designed flat routes as an H-back.
Therefore, it should come as little surprise that Winston has made a concerted effort to build both trust and on-field synergy with his top tight end, adding a significant pass-catching option alongside receiver Malik Nabers.
With the Giants’ Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints fast approaching, Likely is certainly looking to add to his 33 receptions, the most ever by a tight end in his first five games with the Giants, as well as his four touchdowns. To do so, both he and Winston must keep proving the naysayers wrong.
“I feel like every player in the game has good, bad moments and plays that you want back,” Likely said. “But Jameis is a great quarterback. I mean, I feel like in the second half (of Week 5 vs. Commanders), you guys (saw) exactly what Jameis is capable of doing in this league and the offense is capable of doing as well. And I feel like that’s the trajectory we’re trying to go day in and day out.”
In the final analysis, Giants fans everywhere are hoping that trajectory points toward the team’s first playoff appearance since 2022.

title: Giants Injury Report: Six Players Get Game Designations Ahead of Saints
full_text:
The assigned game participation statuses to six players on Friday ahead of their Week 6 home game against the New Orleans Saints. That is the most injury designations the Giants have had this season.
Tight end Theo Johnson (neck), safety Tyler Nubin (neck) and cornerback Colton Hood (concussion) have all been declared out for the contest.
Johnson’s absence means Thomas Fidone II, who has been a healthy scratch through the first four games of the season before finally getting a suit last week, will see a larger role on offense this Sunday.
“Oh, he could help us. He could help us,” head coach John Harbaugh said of Fidone. “He’s had great practices, runs good routes, and played well on special teams last week. Thomas is ready to play, as he showed last week.”
Johnson’s status is also worth monitoring in future weeks, given that he went from a limited participant on Wednesday and Thursday to being kept out of practice on Friday.
The Giants are getting safety Jason Pinnock back for the week after he missed last week due to a concussion.
Pinnock appeared to have quietly passed Nubin on the depth chart for a starting job, but the concussion he suffered two weeks ago gave Nubin a mulligan last week.
Three key Giants are listed as questionable for Sunday: both starting offensive tackles, Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) and Andrew Thomas (groin), and starting outside linebacker Abdul Carter (calf).
All three were limited in practice Friday, an upgrade after they were held out Wednesday and Thursday. The feeling is that both tackles should be good to go for Sunday. If not, rookie J.C. Davis will get the nod at left tackle, where he played well in the preseason, and Marcus Mbow will start at right tackle.
Carter’s status is also worth monitoring. He’s been a big part of the defensive pass rush. With the Giants already missing Brian Burns for the rest of the season due to an ACL injury, not having Carter would be a huge blow to a pass rush that has started to click over the last couple of weeks.
Bold denotes a change in status.
* Reserve list; currently in 21-day practice window.

title: Giants Coach Explains Why He Still Trusts Dominic Zvada After Rough Day
full_text:
New York Giants kicker Dominic Zvada has enjoyed the kind of success few rookies achieve.
In New York’s first four games, Zvada connected on all nine field goal attempts and went 5-for-5 on extra points. One might say that he was Big Blue’s version of “Mr. Perfect.”
Unfortunately, Zvada’s flawless streak ended in the Giants’ Week 5, 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
While the Michigan product did make two field goals (from 51 and 56 yards, respectively) and went 3-for-3 on extra-point tries, he missed three from 50 yards (first quarter), 57 yards (second quarter) and 46 yards (overtime). The last of those would have given the Giants a 30-27 lead.
As a result, Zvada will need to fight through adversity for the first time in his brief NFL career.
Fortunately for both the Giants and their rookie kicker, assistant head coach/special teams coordinator Chris Horton believes that the 22-year-old is well-equipped to meet the challenge.
“We believe in him, we trust him, and we have confidence in him,” Horton told reporters earlier this week.
“It was a great learning experience. Just a couple of little small, little technique things that we’re going to work on to make sure that we get cleaned up.”
Head coach John Harbaugh said Wednesday that the issue stemmed from Zvada’s plant leg.
In five games this season, Zvada has gone 8-for-8 on extra points and 11-for-14 on field goal attempts. Including his nine-point game against Washington, Zvada now leads all rookies in points scored with 41, the fourth-most by a Giant in franchise history through the first five games of his career.
Additionally, Zvada’s 56-yarder in the third quarter of New York’s Week 5 tie moved him into a tie with former Giant Ali Haji-Sheikh (in 1983) for the longest made field goal by a rookie in team history.
And Zvada, despite the misses, is currently tied with three other kickers for the most field goals made from 50+ yards, with five.
Based on that résumé alone, Horton’s faith in his young kicker is seemingly well-deserved.
Yet the Giants assistant head coach is further encouraged by Zvada’s resolve to improve, and he makes a point of encouraging the rookie along the way.
“From a confidence standpoint, you just have to remind him that he is damn good,” Horton said.
“That’s one of the things I think: when you believe in your players again, and you remind them that they’re here for a reason and you trust in them. You’ve just got to remind them of those things. From a confidence standpoint, that’s solely on him and him understanding that I can go out there and I can do this.”
For Zvada, the ensuing days will be about refining his fundamentals. Both Horton and Harbaugh have vowed to work with the rookie on his plant placement and other fixable mechanics, issues he struggled with in Week 5.
Zvada’s first miss (a 50-yard attempt in the first quarter) was attributed to a high snap, which disrupted his timing. On his overtime misfire, Zvada’s plant leg (left) appeared to slip after it was extended. The result was a wide kick to the left.
Having identified Zvada’s recent struggles as “fixable,” Horton is willing to give the undrafted rookie the benefit of the doubt, based on his body of work.
“We judge by consistency,” Horton explained. “This kid was nine-for-nine before he came into this game. He missed three field goals. Yeah, it’s not our standard. It’s not where we want to be, but we do understand that this guy will make kicks. You watch all these kicks from across the league; these things are happening with big-time players. It happens.
“Sometimes we go back to, ‘Hey, why did this happen?’” he revealed. “And it’s foot-to-ball, foot-to-ball. All these things have to be consistent for us to get consistent results where the ball’s going in between the uprights.”
Zvada and the Giants will look to get back on track during their Week 6 matchup with the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford. Kickoff is set for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Giants Scouting Report: What to Expect From the Saints’ Offense
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ defense has played winning football in four of the first five weeks of the season, but it hasn’t started well in many contests.
That could be a problem against a New Orleans Saints offense that can score on any team in the league. The Giants shouldn’t rely on in-game adjustments to succeed.
The Giants have to do a better job of entering the game with a plan of action that keeps points off the board.
Let’s take a look at the New Orleans Saints’ offense and what Big Blue fans should expect from them on Sunday.
Like many teams in the NFL, the Saints’ base personnel is 11 personnel, utilizing a tight end and three receivers.
Under second-year head coach Kellen Moore and offensive coordinator Doug Nussmeier, 11 personnel accounts for approximately 60% of the Saints’ offensive snaps.
In addition to 11 personnel, they use 12 personnel for more run-heavy or bigger-protection plays, using it 25-30% of the time. This gives them two-way run-pass options.
They also use situational 21 personnel, bringing in an extra running back instead of a tight end. Under center, they use split-back and offset sets to create matchup problems between linebackers and running backs.
The Saints ranked 28th in rushing in 2025, and they’re even worse this season. They average only 81.8 yards per game and a paltry 3.5 yards per carry.
They average a rushing touchdown per game, which isn’t bad, but it doesn’t reflect the explosive nature of the New Orleans rushing attack in past seasons. They have been a running back-by-committee unit, and no one player has stood out so far.
They are a wide-zone, outside-zone rushing team that wants to get the defense flowing east and west so they can find open cutback lanes.
They will also utilize some gap schemes and pull concepts to complement their wide zone. They run a ton of pre-snap motion and use condensed split formations to help them attack the perimeter.
The passing offense looked promising early in the season, but over six games, quarterback Tyler Shough’s performance looks eerily similar to that of 2025’s regular-season starter, Spencer Rattler.
They have explosive elements to attack and legitimate receiving weapons. Still, their rankings suggest a team that passes the ball a lot but produces only a mid-tier performance.
They rank second in the NFL in passing attempts per game at 41 while averaging only 240 yards per game. Their 6.3 yards per attempt ranks 25th in the league. Although they are tied for ninth with nine touchdowns, they have thrown five interceptions and have been sacked 13 times.
The Saints’ passing tree comes directly off their wide-zone mesh, letting them run action with rollouts, sprintouts, and naked boots to give Shough half-field reads, high-low reads, and flood concepts that work the sidelines.
Center Erik McCoy remains the anchor of this offensive line. He is a top-five center in the league, and he’s adept at setting protection and being a factor whenever the team wants to run downhill on the interior.
He is the catalyst for success on the offensive line. When healthy, he boosts the entire unit; when he struggles, the entire unit struggles.
Chris Olave is their clear-cut No. 1 weapon on offense. He’s one of the best wide receivers in the game because he can be explosive at every level.
He combines elite separation with top-tier route manipulation, and he has a smooth second gear to attack intermediate openings. He knows when to run through or sit down in lanes, but he can also blow the top off a defense.
Alvin Kamara may not be what he used to be, but he is still a red-zone threat with a nose for the end zone.
Tight end Juwan Johnson is in a similar vein to the Giants’ Isaiah Likely: a big, athletic slot guy who can be a matchup problem for defenses.
Receiver Chris Olave enters the weekend having missed practices due to an acute illness. He should be able to go, but he may not have the stamina he normally has when healthy.
Running back Alvin Kamara is dealing with a back issue that has limited him in practice throughout the past few weeks.
Offensive guard Jeremiah Wright is in the concussion protocol and has been working through it. He progressed back to full participation but has not been fully cleared yet.
Tyler Shough has an injury to his non-throwing hand. He’s been a full participant in practice, but it is worth noting. Let’s see whether it affects how he holds the ball.
What the Saints can do through the air with their multi-level passing attack would be a problem for the Giants if not for the one-dimensional nature of their offense. Because the Saints don’t offer much resistance as a downhill rushing attack, their outside-zone and wide-zone plays play right into the Giants’ athleticism.
The Giants need to keep the Saints throwing the ball because they’ve been very good at taking the ball away and creating pressure to make the quarterback uncomfortable.
They should turn Shough into the primary rushing option, since he’s athletic enough to do it but not explosive enough to hit the Giants for home runs like Jayden Daniels did last week.
Ultimately, if the Saints are forced into a dink-and-dunk offense, they will eventually make mistakes and let the Giants’ defense exploit them.

title: Jets Have 3 Clear Advantages Over Patriots Going into Week 6
full_text:
No one expects the New York Jets to walk into Foxborough this weekend and upset the New England Patriots.
New York is coming off a three-win season while the Patriots are coming off a Super Bowl appearance. The Jets have played inconsistent football to begin the year while New England is on a two-game winning streak.
But stranger things have happened across the NFL. New York has the tools in place to pull off said upset.
And they have an advantage in three key areas to make sure it sticks.
The name of Sunday's game is pressure. It's true that Patriots quarterback Drake Maye is very good against the blitz. That won't matter so long as the Jets are able to get consistent pressure on the young signal-caller with their four downlinemen.
From David Bailey to Will McDonald to Jowon Briggs, New York needs to get pressure throughout Sunday. The good news is that the Patriots offense is still somewhat of a weakness for the team. They are dealing with a number of injuries and while the hobbled group has stayed afloat over the last couple of weeks, there's an advantage here for the Jets to exploit.
If New York gets the kind of rush production they got against Cleveland, it could stymie the entire offensive gameplan for the Patriots.
Christian Gonzalez should be good to go for Sunday's contest. If New England was smart, they would have him travel with Jets star receiver Garrett Wilson throughout the game.
New York needs to consistently feed targets for Wilson throughout Sunday. The best way to do that is by getting him in the slot and in off coverage. So long as the Jets give Wilson space to move, they'll be able to get chunk plays and positive influences across the offense.
Wilson is an ascending talent and someone who seems to be taking the true moniker of a top-10 receiver. Beating up Gonzalez and New England's other corners is just the next step for him going forward.
The Patriots currently sit at 19th in the league in turnovers forced this season. While they can be opportunistic, it just isn't something they are known for this year.
That's a good thing for the Jets offense, even without some of their key players in the game. Geno Smith has yet to throw an interception this season, and has played very well compared to last year's struggles with the Las Vegas Raiders.
If New York doesn't turn the ball offensively, it will give them an edge, especially since the Patriots have a quarterback tied for the league-lead in interceptions so far this season.
Winning the turnover battle is more important than ever in a game like this.

title: Joseph Ossai Is Becoming a Bigger Jets Offseason Regret With Each Passing Week
full_text:
After beating the Browns 17-12 last Sunday, the New York Jets enter Week 6 looking to accomplish something they haven’t done since 2023: win consecutive games.
This won’t be easy, as the Jets face the Patriots in the team’s first divisional showdown of the season. New England, led by quarterback Drake Maye, has been red-hot over the past two weeks. However, if Gang Green wins these three matchups, they could leave Gillette Stadium with a victory.
Unfortunately, the Jets will have to do so without a few of their key players, including edge rusher Joseph Ossai. Head coach Aaron Glenn ruled the five-year veteran from Texas out on Friday after Ossai missed Wednesday and Thursday’s practices with an ankle injury he suffered against Cleveland (h/t Rich Cimini).
Out for Sunday: Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Joseph Ossai and Dylan Parham. Kenyon Sadiq will be full practice today and is finishing his concussion protocol, per Glenn. #Jets
Ossai has appeared in just three of the Jets’ six games this season. He previously dealt with a plantar fascia issue, which forced him to miss the first two contests this season.
In the games he's played, Ossai has been underwhelming, recording nine tackles, seven of them in one game, and zero pressures in 107 defensive snaps.
Although it’s still early, the Ossai signing is already starting to look like a questionable move by the Jets’ brass.
After giving up the fourth-most rushing yards (139.5) and recording the second-fewest sacks last season, upgrading the defensive line was one of New York’s top offseason priorities.
GM Darren Mougey brought in Ossai to help address these needs, signing the former Bengal to a three-year, $34.5 million contract.
The 26-year-old came off his best season with Cincinnati, registering 43 total tackles, five sacks, and 43 pressures. While Ossai displayed potential as a pass rusher, the Jets primarily brought him in to strengthen their run defense.
Last season, Ossai recorded 13 stops and earned a 70.7 run-defense grade, per Pro Football Focus, ranking 25th among 115 qualifying edge rushers.
With New York, he’s been ineffective as a pass rusher and against the run, earning a 50.9 pass-rush grade and a 54.3 run-defense grade, struggling in both areas despite limited playing time.
Ossai still has plenty of time to turn things around, but it’s hard to feel optimistic when other edge rushers whom the Jets could’ve signed are playing important roles for their respective teams.
Derick Hall and Dre’Mont Jones signed contracts in a similar price range and have been playing well so far.
Hall, who re-signed with the Seahawks on a three-year, $42 million contract, has been a reliable rotational contributor, recording 13 total tackles, two sacks, 13 pressures, and three stops. Although his production hasn’t drawn as much attention as other players on Seattle’s talented defensive line, Hall has been a quality contributor.
Jones, meanwhile, signed a three-year, $36.5 million contract with the Patriots and has emerged as a key contributor. Jones has been the team’s best player against the run, per PFF , earning a 77.6, which ranks 11th among 106 qualifying edge rushers. He’s also been an impactful addition to New England’s pass rush, tying for second on the team in pressure with 14.
With Glenn listing Ossai as week-to-week and Braiden McGregor out for the season, New York could start giving Nate Lynn some reps . The former undrafted free agent was a preseason standout, recording eight total tackles and three sacks in two games.
However, if the Jets pull off an upset against the Patriots, they could explore the trade market to bolster the defensive line. Improving to 3-3 would give New York more incentive to invest in its playoff chances, whereas it would be less inclined to surrender a draft pick if they drop to 2-4.
Regardless of how they address their immediate needs, moving on from Ossai won’t be something they do, even if his play doesn’t improve. After this season, his cap hit jumps from $5.46 million to $12.25 million in 2027, per Spotrac , while releasing him before June 1 would cost the team $17.25 million in dead cap.
For now, New York will hope Ossai can return to the field soon and start playing at the level of his contract.

title: Jets Trade Deadline Big Board: Realistic Targets, Possible Sells, & More
full_text:
At 2-3, it's still too early to determine if the Jets intend to be buyers or sellers ahead of November's NFL trade deadline. Much can change over the next month.
But as we get closer to the Nov. 10 deadline, the team's improved play could help the organization push to be more aggressive going forward. Whether that means accumulating more draft capital or acquiring proven talent is up to the outcomes of the coming games.
With that, it's time to break down players the Jets could target in a potential deadline deal, as well as those Gang Green could ship out if the bottom falls out .
Here are the list of opponents the Jets will face between now and the trade deadline next month
A 2-2 mark would put the organization at 4-5 and well on its way to a significantly improved record from the year before. If the Jets reach that mark, then that could be the perfect sign for general manager Darren Mougey to make a move.
New York has big needs along the defensive line, including tackle, edge rusher, and even at linebacker. There should be plenty of names that fit that mold.
For whom, though? Here are some realistic targets the Jets could look at:
If the bottom falls out for the Eagles with so many injuries , they could look to trade away assets that they know they won't be able to retain. After extending Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, it's clear that the Eagles see Ojomo as the odd man out.
Ojomo could see a contract similar to the one Milton Williams got from the Patriots (four years, $104 million, per Spotrac ). He's an ascending young player with plenty of upside. New York may have to give up a third-round pick, but it would be worth it to help bring in a plug-and-play starter on their defensive line.
Daron Payne, DT (Commanders)
It's a similar situation with Commanders tackle Daron Payne. The former Pro Bowler could be moved if Washington continues to lose, and that could lead the Jets to bring in another veteran presence for their defensive line.
Remember, David Onyemata has been lost for most of the season after dealing with core muscle surgery. New York has missed both his veteran presence and his ability to stop the run, two things Payne could actually help with.
Given his age (29), Payne probably cost even less compared to a young player like Ojomo.
Josh Sweat, OLB (Cardinals)
It's well documented that Josh Sweat wants out of Arizona . It's also well documented that the Jets have a pass rush that needs to improve. Kinglsey Enagbare has been a solid free-agent pickup, but with Joseph Ossai injured again, that leaves a hole in the group.
Acquiring a player like Sweat would give the team a consistent pass rusher who is much better against the run than people realize.
If things fall apart for the Jets over the next month, they could also move on from some players they won't be re-signing during the offseason. Here are a couple of names to keep an eye on:
I've been on record saying the Jets should try everything in their power to extend Dane Belton . For Andre Cisco, though, the veteran is more expendable. New York could get him for a late-round draft selection and still have a solid safety room going into 2027.
Kingsley Enagbare has been a revelation early on his one-year deal with the Jets. He's up to two sacks on the year but has been impactful in every game he has played, recording 12 pressures , according to Pro Football Focus .
Enagbare could be someone the team tries to get a mid-round pick for if they can't rack up a few wins over the coming weeks.
Harrison Phillips is a building block in the eyes of the Jets, but if New York is out of contention again, it may behoove the team to try to get draft capital for the defensive tackle on the open market. Remember, Phillips is a free agent after this year , so he very well may leave the team in a few months anyway.
Getting something for him, especially if the team is noncompetitive over the next few weeks, is a forward-thinking choice.

title: Friday's Jets Practice Notebook: Good Injury News, Eyes on the Pats & More in Week 6
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — You don't need Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson to tell you how big Sunday's contest against the Patriots is for Gang Green.
A victory moves New York to 3-3 and arguably their most significant win as a franchise in years. A loss wouldn't sink their season, but it would highlight that the team perhaps isn't as far ahead as many fans would have hoped at this point.
Before the team takes the field in Foxborough, though, the Jets had another Friday practice. It's time to open the notebook to see where the organization is heading .
Let's start with the good news on the injury front.
New York is expected to have rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. back on the field with the team after missing the last few weeks with an ankle injury. Dane Belton, Kenyon Sadiq, and Kiko Mauigoa are all expected to be able to play as well.
For Sadiq, the first-round tight end still needs to pass the next phase of concussion protocol, but there's hope he will in time for Sunday's game.
New York will, however, remain without Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Dylan Parham, and Joseph Ossai, as all have been designated as "week-to-week" according to head coach Aaron Glenn. That said, the coach did say there was some hope that all four players may return to practice next week.
Getting Cooper and Sadiq on the field would be massive for a Jets passing offense that has struggled in recent weeks. At the very least, though, it should give New York a chance to see more of their talented rookie class in action against a tough opponent.
Sunday's contest won't be easy for the Jets. The Patriots have a top-10 defensive unit in almost every category across the board. With Cooper expected to return to the field, New York's passing offense is expected to get a boost.
But that doesn't mean the team is going to be throwing the ball to start against the Jets' arch rival, according to Glenn.
The Jets have not hidden the fact that they want to be a run-first team. That said, it could be seen as a mistake for the team to openly talk about running the football effectively against a Patriots defense that looks for any advantage it can. New England should expect to do everything in their power to stop Gang Green's rushing attack.
Even after a career game from Braelon Allen in last week's win over Cleveland.
"I thought Braelon did a hell of a job," Glenn said of the team's rushing performance. "The whole line and the run concepts that we had... I thought was pretty good."
Right or wrong, the Jets are going to push the run game on Sunday. Time will tell whether being open about it will work.
New York understands that the season is not made or broken by the outcome of Sunday's game. That said, a potential win could fundamentally shift how the team is perceived in the NFL.
Not just as a possible playoff team, but one that seems to be ending the Jets' demons across their division .
Since 2011, the Jets are 25-65 against AFC East opponents. They have beaten the Patriots in Foxborough just once during that stretch. Last season, New York was 0-6 against their biggest rivals in the division.
And while it certainly weighed on fans, a different approach was felt by the team's head coach.
"It was more or less just the season weighed on me. It didn't matter who we lost to," Glenn said. "I don't look at it as more as just division games. I look at it more as just winning games. Because I think at the end of the day, that's what this is all about."
If the Jets are going to prove to the NFL that they are, in fact, improved from the years of struggles they have seen, then winning divisional contests, even against the Patriots, will be massive.
The Jets have been penalized the second most of any other team in the league this season. Some fans point to the team's lack of discipline. Others wonder if this franchise-consistent problem will ever be fixed.
Glenn and the offense, though, have the right mindset. Other teams like the Bills, Seahawks, Ravens, and Packers are all close to the Jets' penalty totals. The difference between the Jets and these playoff contenders is the fact they haven't been able to recover from a mistake.
And that's something the Jets are working on.
Penalties are going to happen in the NFL. Pre-snap and in-game penalties are just things that are dealt to every team. The difference is that good teams are able to recover from a false start or a hold, and bad teams are not.
So far this season, the Jets have been unable to recover whenever a mistake is made. That needs to change going forward.

title: David Bailey's DROY Case Is Undeniable (Here's How the Jets' Rookie Can Pull Away in the Race)
full_text:
As the Jets prepare for their first AFC East opponent of the season, when they face the Patriots on Sunday, all eyes will be on Gang Green to see if they can end a pitiful trend against divisional competition amid a combined 25-65 record dating back to 2011.
To pull off the upset, New York's defense will have a huge say in that, after being the most dominant unit on the field in the 17-12 win over the Browns last Sunday. The Jets combined for eight sacks and clearly went into the game with the intention of loading the box and creating constant pressure on Deshaun Watson, a decision that proved to be the right call by head coach Aaron Glenn .
Someone who was instrumental in that success was rookie EDGE David Bailey, going off for three sacks, seven tackles (five solo), three tackles for loss, and four quarterback hits. That performance led to him earning AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors and well-deserved recognition.
That said, he still has a lot to prove if he truly wants to live up to the No. 2 draft pick.
It was a relatively slow start for Bailey, but he continues to build his Defensive Rookie of the Year case with each passing week, and his breakout against the Browns was a key first step toward winning that award by season's end. His stock is already skyrocketing as New York's best pass rusher, and his Week 5 performance was his first real reminder why.
Bailey has made it clear that he is still adjusting to his role in the NFL , as he has had to adjust to no longer being an every-down pass rusher like he was accustomed to at Texas Tech. While his run defense was an area he needed to improve, Bailey has made strides in that area and has continued to dominate the pass rush (h/t NFL) after leading college football in sacks last season.
David Bailey was a man on a mission in Week 5 🔥 @Pepsi pic.twitter.com/DKOYWjlsLg
According to Pro Football Focus , Bailey has the 43rd-ranked overall grade (68.6) and the 10th-most pressures (20) out of 106 qualified edge defenders in the league. His pass-rush grade (59.5) is 69th, but most impressively, his run-defense grade (76.1) is 16th for a player who has been a pleasant surprise in that particular area. In fact, that grade is even higher than fifth overall pick Arvell Reese (74.0), who was already expected to become a three-down defender for the Giants.
So far, Bailey is averaging four pressures per game, putting him on pace for 68—including a season-high nine vs. the Browns. For reference, he finished with 39 or fewer in each of his three years at Stanford before racking up 81 in his lone campaign at Texas Tech.
There is no doubt that Bailey has been the best rookie on this Jets team so far , and he appears to only be getting started with his high motor and explosiveness off the snap that make him so hard to defend.
Looking at the upcoming schedule, everything is in front of Bailey to compete for the DROY award, especially as certain sportsbooks are beginning to favor him over the likes of fellow defenders Reese and Dolphins linebacker Jacob Rodriguez.
As of Friday afternoon, DraftKings Sportsbook lists Bailey as the current favorite to be named DROY (+200) over Reese (+300) and Rodriguez (+350). With Commanders LB Sonny Styles (+1000) the only other player with odds better than +2000, it looks like a three-man race unless something changes between now and January.
While Rodriguez (57) and Reese (43) have more total tackles than Bailey (25) so far, they have only one sack combined. Granted, they both have an interception through the first five games as well, but neither has had the same overall impact in pass rush as Bailey has up to this point.
Look no further than Sunday's road trip to Gillette Stadium for Bailey's next opportunity to improve his case for the DROY award. The Patriots are banged up on the offensive line, including the questionable status of starting left tackle Will Campbell (right knee). Combine that with QB Drake Maye's turnover-prone start to the 2026 season, and there is every reason to believe that Bailey can be just as impactful again this weekend.
After that, the Jets return home for two games against the winless Dolphins and the surprising Raiders. Both QBs—Malik Willis and Kirk Cousins—have combined for eight interceptions and have been sacked 22 times. In other words, Bailey has an opportunity to cement his frontrunner status in the next three games before a two-game stretch against the Chiefs and Bills ensues.
Bailey made a strong statement against the Browns and showed that the 2026 Defensive Rookie of the Year Award starts and stops with him. If he keeps performing at (or even improves on) his current level and makes a major impact on the field, Bailey could pull away in this race and prove the Jets made the right decision when they selected him second overall in April.

title: 3 Key Matchups Will Decide Jets’ Week 6 Outcome vs. Patriots (Gang Green Needs a Braelon Allen Encore)
full_text:
The Jets head into Week 6 trying to build on last week’s victory over the Browns. This will be a challenge, however, as they’ll be heading to Gillette Stadium to take on the Patriots.
Even with the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick era behind them, the Patriots continue to dominate this rivalry, with New York going 2-10 against New England since 2020. Although leaving with a win will be difficult, especially with the Patriots turning things around in the last two games, it’s not impossible.
If Gang Green can win these three matchups, they’ll give themselves a chance to pull off a road upset and earn back-to-back victories for the first time since 2023.
Unlike last year, the Jets have been ineffective at running the ball, ranking 22nd in rushing yards per game (94) and tied for 25th in yards per attempt (3.6). Despite their inefficiencies, their victories have relied heavily on pounding the ball.
In their three losses, the Jets ran the ball on 31.3%, 37.5%, and 43.8% of their plays, averaging 61.3 rushing yards per game. In their two victories, however, they ran the ball on 48.5% and 62% of their plays, averaging 143 rushing yards per game.
This trend makes establishing the run a priority against the Patriots, even without Breece Hall, who’s missed the team’s last three practices before officially being ruled out by the Jets on Friday, reported by ESPN 's Rich Cimini.
Out for Sunday: Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Joseph Ossai and Dylan Parham. Kenyon Sadiq will be full practice today and is finishing his concussion protocol, per Glenn. #Jets
Braelon Allen will likely take on the bulk of the workload again . Allen played a key role in the Jets' Week 5 win over the Browns, setting career highs in rushing attempts (24) and rushing yards (116) and adding a touchdown.
Running the ball won’t be easy against the Patriots' defense, as they rank sixth in rushing yards allowed per game (90.8) and are tied for 13th in yards per carry allowed (4). Still, the Jets can’t afford to abandon the ground game if they struggle to find success early.
Pounding the football will be crucial to taking pressure off Geno Smith and giving the Patriots another dimension to keep New England’s defense guessing. With Garrett Wilson being the team’s only reliable receiving option, maintaining a balanced attack will be crucial.
The more the New York feeds Allen, the more opportunities he will have to break through for explosive runs. That’s exactly what happened last week against the Brown, as the bruising back from Wisconsin displayed his big-play potential, recording five runs of 10 or more yards.
If the Jets remain patient and continue feeding him the ball, Allen could eventually break through for a big gain. Although the Jets' offensive line hasn’t been great at creating running lanes, ranking 14th in run blocking , per Pro Football Focus, one play can spark the ground game.
At 6'1" and 250 lbs, Allen has the size that makes him hard to bring down and the speed to break away from defenders. If New York’s offensive line opens running lanes for him at the second level, Allen could replicate similar success on the ground and keep New England’s defense on its heels.
Two weeks ago, this matchup looked more attainable for the Jets, with Drake Maye struggling mightily through the first three weeks. The third-year quarterback from North Carolina threw for 585 yards, one touchdown, and six interceptions in New England’s first three games.
But in the last two games, Maye has started to look like the MVP runner-up he was last season, throwing for 643 yards, seven passing touchdowns, and just one interception. He’s also remained elite against the blitz, completing 71.7% of his passes, throwing four touchdowns and an interception.
To limit Maye success through the air, New York must make some adjustments to its scheme.
With head coach Aaron Glenn taking over as defensive play caller, the Jets have taken an aggressive approach, ranking fourth in blitz rate at 39%. They’ll have to switch things up against Maye and rely on their front four to generate pressure rather than consistently sending extra rushers.
Maye has been far less effective when defenses don’t blitz, completing 62.9% of his passes for one touchdown and six interceptions. When defenses sit back, he can hold the ball too long while searching for big plays, leading to costly mistakes and 14 sacks.
This puts added pressure on the Jets’ secondary to stay disciplined in coverage and limit downfield opportunities, where Maye is most dangerous. With A.J. Brown potentially making his return, Gang Green could face an even greater challenge downfield.
New York can match Brown’s physicality with Azareye’h Thomas, who’s impressed in coverage this year, earning a 74.4 coverage grade, per PFF , ranking 11th among 104 qualifying cornerbacks .
Ultimately, the Jets’ ability to contain Maye will depend on how their secondary plays in coverage. If New York can prevent the Patriots’ receivers from creating separation, it could force Maye to hold onto the ball long enough for the pass rush to get to him.
Staying with Brown and the Patriots’ other deep threats could also create interceptions, which they’ll need to stay in the game.
For the most part, Smith has been a good game-managing quarterback. The 14-year veteran impressed with his efficiency in the first three games, completing 75.5% of his passes for 783 yards, four touchdowns, and zero interceptions.
While Smith kept the ball out of harm’s way in the last two games, he hasn’t been as effective, completing 55.5% of his passes for 301 yards and two touchdowns. Although injuries to several key playmakers have played a role, Smith has been less aggressive in pushing the ball downfield, attempting just 12 passes of 20 yards or more this season.
However, Smith’s struggles aren’t entirely on him. Aside from Wilson, the rest of the Jets’ receiving corps has struggled to get open , forcing Smith to wait for throwing windows to develop. He’s tied 14th in time to throw at 2.93 seconds and has been sacked 16 times through five games, the third-most in the league.
This is where New England’s pass rush could make life miserable for Smith. The Patriots rank ninth in blitz percentage (36.1%) and are tied for 15th in quarterback pressure rate (36.7%), according to NFL Next Gen Stats.
Although their pass rush hasn’t been as effective, with New England tying for 12th in sacks with 11, defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr could test Smith early by dialing up some blitzes.
If the Jets want to improve their chances of winning, Smith must make quick decisions with the ball and avoid holding the ball too long. Screen and quick passes to Isaiah Williams and,if he plays,  Kenyon Sadiq could help counter the Patriots’ blitzes and give the offense opportunities to move the chains.
Smith must also continue to target Wilson early and often. Reich must build on last week’s game plan against the Browns and get Wilson more involved in the slot. The five-year veteran made plays with the ball in his hands last week, recording a season-high 55 yards after the catch.
Even if cornerback Christian Gonzalez plays and lines up against him, Smith shouldn’t shy away from targeting his best playmaker. Getting Wilson the ball in space rather than relying on him to make contested catches downfield could help New York move the ball downfield.

title: Jets' Ideal Approach for Omar Cooper Jr. Injury Return Becoming Clear in Week 6
full_text:
Football can be a numbers game sometimes. For fans, the best way to judge if a unit is playing well is cross-checking stats across the league.
If we judge the New York Jets based on stats alone offensively, then only one conclusion can be brought:
They haven't nearly been good enough.
New York ranks as the 23rd-best passing attack, 26th overall, and 27th in points. Part of the reason for that is the unit has been decimated with injuries to key players. Running back Breece Hall, left guard Dylan Parham, wide receiver AD Mitchell, and tight end Mason Taylor have all missed significant time to begin the year.
But the cavalry is close to arriving. In the case of New York's passing unit, the return of one of their top rookies could greatly impact how the group looks moving forward.
New York activated first-round rookie Omar Cooper Jr. off of the short-term IR list this week. Over the last two practices, the Indiana prospect has been "limited" on the field. New York has been clear for Cooper:
They won't force him onto the field unless he is ready, and he needs to pass through a series of rep tests in practice to do so.
"He's a really good player, but you never want any rookie to actually miss time because the reps are valuable for these guys," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "And I think all of our rookies that's been getting these reps have been valuable."
Cooper made a major impact in his lone appearance this season. Against the Tennessee Titans in Week 1, he caught a short pass and raced 30 yards downfield to set the team up for their first touchdown of the game. Unfortunately for him, he suffered an ankle injury that has cost him the last four weeks.
Now that he is healthy, though, the Jets should not be patient with him. They should not hesitate to give him a full load of plays going into Week 6 and beyond. There's no guarantee he plays against the New England Patriots on Sunday, of course, but if he does, he should get the full work of a WR2.
Why? Because he is easily New York's second-best receiving option when on the field. While the Jets have preached their desire to be patient with rookies, some like David Bailey, have proven to be ready for a large set of plays right away.
Based on Cooper's excellence at Indiana, and his strong training camp, the Jets should treat their first-round receiver the same way. Otherwise, the team will have to trust Tim Patrick or Isaiah Williams to take pressure off of Garrett Wilson.
That just isn't good enough.
And it's why there should be no hesitation to get their rocket rookie the ball as early and as often as possible when he gets back on the game field.

title: How Week 6 Could Alter Jets' Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
The New York Jets are in rare territory going into Sunday's contest. With the trade deadline less than a month away, Gang Green must decide whether to be buyers, sellers, or stand pat with the current roster they have.
At 2-3, it's hard to determine exactly which way the Jets will go. After all, while they have been competitive in some games, they have yet to show they can beat top competition in order to place themselves in playoff contention.
That all can change on Sunday.
A showdown against their archrival New England Patriots could very well determine which side of the coin the Jets will fall on: buyers or sellers.
New York knows how important Sunday's game is. It's not just a chance to get to .500 against the defending conference champions. It's the first chance the team has to show how far they have come as a roster and a coaching staff.
A win in Foxborough would be the signature win for head coach Aaron Glenn. It would quiet a lot of the animosity fans have for him. A victory would also be a sign for owner Woody Johnson to know that he ended up picking the right head coach.
"There's a premium on this one because it is our first one [in the division]," Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson said on Wednesday. "I don't know how to exactly put it, but it's a big-ass game."
If the team is blown out in any way, shape or form, then there will certainly be something of a letdown. It would show general manager Darren Mougey that the team is not ready for true title contention and they would need more time to actually develop as a roster. It would also show the coaching staff is unable to make up for a talent deficiency against tough competition.
In the sense of the trade deadline, though, a loss would put the team close to the sellers' market. Players who may not be seen as a value to the organization may be moved: performers like Dane Belton, Kingsley Enagbare, or Harrison Phillips could be moved for draft capital.
It may seem like a long shot now, but at this time last year no one thought Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams were both going to be moved. And then they were after a dismal 1-7 start to the year.
If the Jets want to avoid a similar deadline to the one they had last year, they will need to win more games. And the easiest way to get on that board is to beat their arch rival in New England.
Should that happen, New York won't just come away with a massive win, they could reset their entire culture going forward.
